en: May the illustrious Lakṣmīveṅkaṭeśa be ever victorious!
The *Pramāṇapaddhati* composed by the venerable Śrī Jayatīrtha.
Having bowed to the pair of lotus feet of the Lord of Kamalā,
we compose this *Pramāṇapaddhati* for the sake of achieving understanding by the young.
Justification for the commencement of the work:

Although the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth have indeed been stated by the venerable teacher himself, nevertheless, because they were described in profound language and in a scattered manner, they cannot be easily understood by those of dull intellect. Thus [the present work is begun].
For that purpose, this treatise is commenced.

Regarding the exposition of the definition and essential nature: that property which exists pervasively in the subject of definition (*lakṣya*) and does not exist elsewhere is the [defining] property.
A definition (lakṣaṇa) is stated as follows: for example, the possession of a dewlap and so forth is the definition of a cow. For that [definition] exists in all cows and does not exist in non-cows.
[Next is discussed] the nature of the non-definition and its threefold classification.

That which is otherwise, however, is a non-characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*). It is of three kinds: (1) the impossible (*asambhavin*), which does not exist at all in the object to be characterized (*lakṣya*); for example, the possession of a single hoof in a cow. (2) The non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), which, although existing in one part of the object to be characterized, does not exist in another part of it; for example, [the dewlap] in a cow.

The state of being variegated (*śabalatva*) is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*), as it exists elsewhere than in the subject to be defined (*lakṣya*), just like the state of having horns (*viṣāṇitva*). The purpose of knowing the definition is—

The purpose of the knowledge of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is the ascertainment of the object of definition (*lakṣya*) by way of its exclusion from both similar and dissimilar things. For instance, in one who has heard the report, "Devadatta’s house is in this village," there arises the cognition of Devadatta’s house with respect to all the houses situated in that village.

[The relationship] is established. Therefore, when there is a cognition of the definition—"Wherever there is a banner, that is Devadatta’s house"—there arises a definitive determination (*avadhāraṇa*) that "it is this very one, and not another. Alternatively, the purpose of the cognition of the definition is linguistic usage (*śabdavyavahāra*).
Regarding the nature of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*):

once there is knowledge of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) that "that which possesses a dewlap and so forth is a cow," whatever individual (*piṇḍa*) possessing a dewlap one perceives, one understands each of those to be denotable by the word "cow," as long as there remains anything from which it must be distinguished.
To the extent that a single word is to be explained, that is called the "illustrative example" (*lakṣya*).

Regarding the general definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), first of all, the general definition of the means of valid cognition is stated: the means of valid cognition is that which corresponds to reality (*yathārtha*).

"Valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is the indication of the definiendum; "in accordance with the object" (*yathārtham*) is the statement of the definition. This should be understood in the same way for what follows as well. Here, the word *yathā* functions in the sense of "not exceeding" (*anatikrame*). Furthermore, by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that which is sought" (*arthyate*), the word *artha* denotes the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Thus, [valid cognition] is that which exists without exceeding the object of knowledge, precisely as it is situated (*yathāvasthitam*).

The meaning is that it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it takes the object of knowledge as its domain, and not otherwise. Furthermore, this "taking the object of knowledge as its domain" is intended either as being direct, or as being the instrument for directly taking the object of knowledge as its domain; thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding the secondary means of valid cognition (*anupramāṇa*). It is precisely by virtue of taking the object of knowledge as its domain...

There is a distinction between the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*). This is because neither of them directly takes the knowable as its object; furthermore, even though they are causes for that which does directly take the knowable as its object, they lack the status of being the instrument (*sādhana*) thereof. One who possesses valid cognition (*pramā*) is the knower. The object of valid cognition is the object of knowledge. Valid cognition is knowledge that accords with reality (*yathārthajñāna*).
By the inclusion of the term "as it truly is" (*yathārtha*), doubt (*saṃśaya*) and error (*viparyaya*), along with their respective causes, are excluded.

Doubt is knowledge that lacks determination (*anavadhāraṇajñāna*). The inclusion of the term "lack of determination" is for the purpose of excluding correct knowledge and error. The term "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is for the purpose of excluding jars and other non-cognitive objects. Regarding this [correct knowledge], some say that there are five causes: common characteristics (*sādhāraṇadharma*), unique characteristics (*asādhāraṇadharma*), conflicting testimony (*vipratipatti*), perception (*upalabdhi*), and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), which operate in conjunction with the absence of a decisive factor (*nirṇāyakābhāva*). For example:
Having perceived the common property of verticality in the object standing before him— a property shared by both a post and a person—

and having recalled the post and the person, one who desires to know the specific distinction, yet does not perceive the curved hollows and so forth that determine "post-ness," nor the head, hands, and so forth that determine "person-ness."
A wavering cognition of doubt arises, such as: "Is this a post or a person?

Furthermore, for one who perceives the uncommon property of being a specific quality of space (*ākāśa*) in sound, yet lacks the means of definitive determination, doubt occurs: "Is sound eternal or non-eternal?"

For one who observes the disagreement between the Vaiśeṣika and Sāṅkhya schools regarding whether the sense organs (*indriya*) are material (*bhautika*) or immaterial (*abhautika*), and who lacks a means of certain determination, doubt arises as to whether "the sense organs are material or immaterial. This occurs just as when, after digging a well, water is discovered.

In the absence of a definitive means of determination, doubt arises: "Is the water already existing there perceived through the digging of the well, or is it something non-existent that has been produced? Or, for one who has heard the statement "there is a *piśāca* in this banyan tree" and has gone near the tree, when no *piśāca* is perceived there, doubt occurs due to the lack of a determining factor: "Is it [the *piśāca*] actually present..."

Others hold that there are only three causes [of non-apprehension], because the doubt— whether a *piśāca* is not perceived due to the power of invisibility (*antardhāna-śakti*) or whether it simply does not exist—
is included within the common property of both apprehension and non-apprehension; for apprehension occurs only with respect to existing things, such as jars, by means of bringing forth a lamp.

It is observed that for non-existent things, such as a rabbit's horn, non-perception occurs after the operation of causes like a potter; likewise, the non-perception of existent things like Īśvara and so forth is also observed.
We, however, say: even in the case of disagreement regarding uncommon properties (*asādhāraṇadharma*), there exists a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*).

This is the inclusion [of the uncommon reason within the inconclusive]. For an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) is not a cause of doubt by its own nature, because it lacks the capacity to cause the recollection of specific characteristics; rather, it acts only by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
And thus, there is the exclusion of the eternal from the non-eternal, and the exclusion of the non-eternal from the eternal.

That "it is the property of the eternal" is indeed common [to both sides]. Nor is there a rule that it must be characterized by only one common property; rather, the fact that it is apprehended in such-and-such a way is its property in each respective case, and thus even the disagreement (*vipratipatti*) is common.
Error (*viparyaya*) is a distorted determination (*viparītaniścaya*). The term "distorted" excludes correct determination;
"determination" excludes doubtful cognition. And that [error] arises from fallacious perception, inference, and scripture, such as:
"This is silver in what is actually mother-of-pearl," and so forth.
The Refutation of the Views of the Prābhākaras and Others:

The Prābhākaras and others maintain that there is no such thing as false cognition (*ayathārtha-jñāna*). This is not so, because it is established by experience. [For example, one thinks: "For all this time, I [perceived] nothing but mother-of-pearl as silver..."

Furthermore, it is because there is a subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) such as "I have perceived [it]. Regarding the silver that was perceived, the Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that it exists as a real entity in another location;
the Vijñānavādins maintain that it is of the very nature of cognition; and Bhāskara maintains that it exists as something produced at that very moment in that very place.
The proponents of Māyā (Māyāvādins) maintain that it is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, but rather strictly indefinable (*anirvacanīya*).

The Teachers (*Ācāryas*), however, hold that because of the subsequent experience—"the silver appeared as something non-existent"—it is the Śruti itself that appears in the form of an absolutely non-existent silver. This is *anadhyavasāya* (non-determination).
The Vaiśeṣikas maintain that dream is a type of erroneous cognition (*ayathārthajñāna*).

[Regarding the example: "What is the name of this tree?"—this is non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*). However, because the possible alternatives (*koṭis*) are too numerous, it is actually a doubt (*saṃśaya*) whose specific alternatives have not been specified. [This applies to] the exclusion of [the tree] from being a *vaṭa* or other such species.

Even when one sees a *panasa* tree, the cognition that arises—"What is the name of this tree?"—is not a [valid] knowledge at all; rather, it is merely a desire to know the object's designation. Furthermore, even the perception of elephants and such in a dream is indeed real, because elephants and so forth are produced from mental impressions (*vāsanā*). However, the cognition of externality regarding them is precisely an error (*viparyaya*).

In the region of the outer courtyard, even the knowledge of probability— otherwise known as conjecture (*ūha*), in the form "this must be a man"— is indeed nothing but doubt (*saṃśaya*), because it is dominated by one alternative due to the predominance of the cause that leads toward that alternative.
[Therefore,] *tarka* has the nature of inference (*anumāna*).

We shall explain that *tarka* (presumptive reasoning) is indeed nothing other than inference (*anumāna*). If it is argued that the definition of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is over-extensive as it applies to memory (*smṛti*), we say no; for memory also functions as a means of valid knowledge in both worldly and Vedic practice.
[This concludes] the definition of a means of valid knowledge and the refutation of the Mīmāṃsaka position.

Experience (*anubhūti*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The Prābhākaras define experience as knowledge distinct from memory. This definition is incorrect because it is over-extensive, as it includes doubt and error, and under-extensive, as it fails to include memory and the Vedas, which are instruments for producing knowledge of reality as it is.

The definition of the Bhaṭṭas— that the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is the cognition of action (*kriyājñāna*), which establishes a particular manifestation (*prakāśaviśeṣa*) residing in the object of cognition (*prameya*), and which is synonymous with "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) or "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*)—
is also untenable, because [it assumes] a cognizedness distinct from cognition itself.

Because it is impossible [to establish such a creator] due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); because cognitions of objects such as the past lack a substratum and thus cannot be produced by him; and because [the definition] fails to apply (*avyāpti*) to the Vedas and similar texts. Furthermore, their alternative definition—that valid cognition is "knowledge of an object not previously apprehended in that manner"—is also incorrect, as it likewise fails to apply to memory and the Vedas.
The refutation of the Naiyāyika position:

The Naiyāyikas and others maintain that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which establishes correct experience (*samyaganubhava*). That too is incorrect, because it does not extend to knowledge that is already in accordance with reality (*yathārthajñāna*). Udayana [defines it] as "that which is pervaded by valid cognition" (*pramāvyāptam pramāṇam*); that too—
It is incorrect [to define validity] as being pervaded by God’s cognition, because this would be over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*) since it applies to every object of knowledge (*prameya*).
If you argue that what is intended is "being pervaded by a cognition" while being either the means of proof (*sādhana*) or its locus (*āśraya*), we say no;
for the mention of the "locus" (*āśraya*) would be redundant. If you claim it is for the sake of establishing God's own status as a valid cognizer, [we reply: no.

If it is argued [that the suffix -ana denotes the agent], no; for there is no grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) authorizing the word *pramāṇa* in the sense of an agent. Furthermore, it would result in an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) because it would not apply to cognitions that correspond to reality (*yathārtha*). Therefore, it is logical that correspondence to reality (*yāthārthya*) alone is the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The means of valid cognition is twofold: direct perception (*kevala*) and inference (*anupramāṇa*). Among these, a cognition that corresponds to reality—

"Valid cognition alone" (kevalapramāṇam): by "as it truly is" (yathārtham), doubt and the like are excluded; by "cognition" (jñānam), perception is specified. Inferential cognition and verbal cognition, although they are indirect means of knowledge (anupramāṇa) with respect to the object possessing the mark (liṅgin) or the meaning of the sentence, are valid cognitions alone with respect to the mark (liṅga) or the sentence itself; thus, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti).
And this is called "exclusive" (*kevala*) because it directly takes the objects of knowledge as its domain.
That fourfold nature of knowledge is indeed fourfold: the knowledge of Īśvara, the knowledge of Lakṣmī, the knowledge of the yogin, and...
And there is the knowledge of the non-yogi. Among these, the knowledge of Īśvara has all things as its object;

it is invariably true to reality; its nature is beginningless and eternal; it is independent; and it is unsurpassedly clear. However, in the case of Īśvara, this [knowledge] is not universal, even when there is no directed attention (*anālocana*) elsewhere.
The knowledge of Lakṣmī has all things as its object; it is also invariably true. Its nature is beginningless and eternal, and it is dependent solely upon the Lord.
It is inferior [to that knowledge] in terms of clarity. And this clarity, like immediacy, resides in the knowledge itself.
The distinction is not conditioned by the object.
The varieties of yogic cognition are as follows: yogic cognition is that which has attained excellence through the power of yoga; it is of three kinds.

The knowledge of the upright yogi (*ṛjuyogijñāna*), the knowledge of the ultimate yogi (*tāttvikayogijñāna*), and the knowledge of the non-ultimate yogi (*atāttvikayogijñāna*). "Upright" refers to those living beings (*jīva*) who are fit for the state of Brahman. When there is perception of anything other than the Lord (*īśvara*), that resulting knowledge has all things as its object; however, in the case of the Lord himself, it is not universal. That...

It is of two kinds: its essential nature (*svarūpa*) and that which consists of mental modifications (*manovṛtti*). Among these, the essential nature is beginningless and eternal; through the power of yoga, until liberation, it is endowed with an excellence of manifestation; and in the state of liberation, it is of a single uniform mode.
Empirical cognition (*vṛttijñāna*), however, is beginningless in its stream; it is produced by perception and other means of knowledge aided by yoga.

In liberation, it does not exist at all. Both types of cognition are invariably true-to-reality. In the case of the Lord (*īśvara*), however, its object is greater than that of other individual souls (*jīva*). Beyond those are the gods who possess pride regarding their respective principles (*tattva*).

The Realists [maintain]: Given its beginninglessness, even when there is perception other than that of Īśvara, that cognition arising from it has non-universal objects. That too is twofold: internal (svarūpa) and external (bāhya). Its beginninglessness is as previously stated. The internal is always exactly as it is; the external is sometimes not as it is.

Deities and others distinct from that [the Lord] are non-eternal yogis. Since they are beginningless yet other than the Lord, their knowledge is conjoined with limited ignorance. That [knowledge] is also twofold, as before.

In that regard, the beginninglessness of their essential nature (*svarūpa*) is in reference to manifestation (*vyakti*); for others, it is in reference to the arising of a continuous stream (*pravāha*).
The restriction to reality (*yāthārthya-niyama*) and so forth are as previously described.

The various types of non-yogi knowledge belong to those living beings who are distinct from [the yogis] and are thus non-yogis. Apart from the Lord, that knowledge is predominantly characterized by ignorance; it too, as before, is of two kinds and is subject to arising and destruction.

Non-yogins are also of three kinds: those fit for liberation (*mukti-yogya*), the eternally transmigrating (*nitya-saṃsārin*), and those fit for darkness (*tama-yogya*). Among them, the knowledge of the true nature of reality (*svarūpa-jñāna*) is indeed correct for those fit for liberation; for the eternally transmigrating, it is mixed; and for the others, it is indeed incorrect. As for external [knowledge], however, it is of both kinds for all three.

The refutation of the Vaiśeṣika position: The Vaiśeṣikas maintain that valid knowledge (*yathārthajñāna*) is fourfold—arising from the senses, arising from a mark (*liṅga*), memory, and that of the sages (*ārṣa*). This is incorrect, because it fails to include [knowledge] that is eternal and that which is produced by scripture (*āgama*).
Furthermore, it is improper to treat memory as distinct from sensory perception and the knowledge of the sages as distinct from yogic cognition.
The definition of secondary means of valid cognition (*anupramāṇa*):

a secondary means of valid cognition is that which brings about knowledge of an object as it truly is. If one were to say merely "knowledge of an object as it truly is," there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to [erroneous cognitions]. If one were to say merely "knowledge," there would be over-extension to doubt and the like.
Furthermore, there is non-pervasion (avyāpti) regarding perception. If it is stated simply as "the means" (sādhana), there is over-extension (ativyāpti) to axes and the like.
If it is stated as "knowledge that accords with reality" (yathārthajñāna), there is over-extension to mere knowledge and non-pervasion regarding perception.
If it is stated as "the means that accords with reality," there is over-extension to the means for [other forms of] perception. If it is stated as "the means of knowledge" (jñānasādhana)...

There would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to doubt and other such factors in the definition of a means of valid cognition (*sādhana*). If it were stated merely as "the cause of true knowledge," there would be over-extension to the knower (*pramātṛ*) and so forth; therefore, every term [in the definition] is purposeful. Here, what is intended by "means" (*sādhana*) is that class of things immediately following which an effect invariably arises. Consequently, there is no over-extension to accidental coincidences (*yādṛcchikasaṃvādi*).

One might object: it should be stated that "the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is threefold," since the suffix -lyuṭ is prescribed even in the sense of a locus (adhikaraṇa). True; nevertheless, because the word *pramāṇa* is never used in the sense of a locus, that [locus] is not included. Furthermore, in the word *pramāṇa*, the suffix denotes an abstract state (bhāva-sādhana).
The term *karaṇa* has multiple meanings, being derived both as an instrument (*sādhana*) and so forth. In that case, what is the point of stating a common definition?

It is replied: this word does not have an entirely distinct meaning like words such as *akṣa* (die/eye). Rather, since the conformity with the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) is equal in both instances, there is no fault in stating a common definition by relying on their having a single underlying sense.

The types of valid cognition (*anupramāṇa*): valid cognition is threefold—perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and scripture (*āgama*). Among these, perception is the contact of a faultless sense organ with its object. By the word "object" (*artha*), the objects of the senses [are meant].
They are apprehended. Their defects include excessive distance, extreme proximity, subtlety, obstruction, impact by similar substances, lack of manifestation, and similarity, among others.
When these are present, in some cases no cognition arises at all; in other cases, a distorted cognition is produced.
The primary [element] is sixfold, distinguished as the nose, tongue, eye, skin, ear, and mind. Among these, odors and their specific varieties are the objects of the nose;
tastes and their specific varieties are the objects of the tongue; and some [hold that] large, material substances possessing form [are the objects of the eye].

The qualities (guṇas), actions (karmans), and genera (jātis) are the objects of the eye and the skin. Wind and touch are also objects of the skin. Sound is the object of the ear. For these five [senses], the lack of supervision by the mind (mano'nadhiṣṭhitatva) and defects such as cataracts and jaundice are the causes of impairment. However, for the mind, these [defects] arise through its supervision of the external sense organs.
All objects [are included]. The mind (*manas*) is the instrument of memory by its own independence. Its defects are attachment and so forth.

By the word "senses" (*indriya*), the cognitive senses (*jñānendriya*) are meant. That is twofold: the sense that is the nature of the knower (*pramātṛ-svarūpa*) and the elemental (*prākṛta*). Among these, the sense that is the essential nature is called the Witness (*sākṣin*).

Its objects are its own essential nature (*ātmasvarūpa*), its attributes (*dharmas*), ignorance (*avidyā*), the mind (*manas*) and its modifications (*vṛttis*), external sensory cognitions, pleasure and so forth, time, the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), space (*ākāśa*), and the like. And it manifests the knowledge of its own nature.

[Objection: But surely memory lacks correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*). For at the time when an object is remembered in a certain way, it is not actually like that, because its previous state has ceased to exist. [Reply: This is not so, because at the time of the cognition, the object’s being "thus" (*tathātva*) is not what is required for correspondence; rather, [it is the object’s being thus at the time it was originally perceived].

Whatever object is apprehended by a cognition in a certain way, in relation to a particular place and time, its reality consists in being exactly so at that place and time. And in that case, memory apprehends it as "at that time, this was such-and-such. Yet, at that time, it was not the case that it was not such-and-such. Now, [one might object]: [The objection continues: ...is not the past object non-existent? [The answer follows: No, for...

The latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a prior experience is the cause of memory; and that [impression] is held to generate memory only with respect to the object previously experienced. Furthermore, the object was not apprehended by the experience as having its previous state ceased. Therefore, how could memory—produced from a latent impression whose object is identical to that of the experience—[apply] to the object?

One might argue that [recollection] would take [the object] as its domain because its previous state has ceased; but this is not so. This would be the case only if we admitted that recollection is produced solely by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). But it is not so.
Recollection is produced by the mind (*manas*); rather, the mental impression is simply the mind’s contact with that object.

Just as there is a quality born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*) for the senses of a yogi, so too, the mind—assisted by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*)—might produce memory that takes as its object even that which has not been directly experienced, namely, a state from which it has previously ceased;
what fault is there in this? For even the senses, though having only the present as their object, [can perceive the past] through the power of auxiliary factors.

They also take as their object a connection with another time, just as the sense organs, aided by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), produce the means for recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—such as "this is that"—which has as its object a subject qualified by both past and present states. In this case, the ordinary sense organs generate a cognition that is a modification of the mind (*manovṛtti*); therein, there is sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*).

If it is stated that "perception is [the contact] itself," there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the contact between a jar and a cloth. If it is stated that "perception is the contact of the sense organ," there is over-extension to the contact between the eye and space. If it is stated that "[perception is] the contact with the object," there is over-extension as before. Furthermore, there is over-extension in the case of contact with defective objects or by means of defective sense organs.
The term "faultless" (*nirdoṣa*) is included in both cases in order to exclude [invalid cognitions].

Now, it may be objected: perception is a specific instrument (*karaṇa*), and an instrument must possess an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*). For example, the contact with wood is the intermediate operation of the axe, which is the instrument for cutting.
True. Here too, the sense organ (*indriya*) possesses the nature of an instrument (*karaṇa*). Its intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) is the contact with the object (*arthasaṃnikarṣa*).

In that regard, when there is an intention to emphasize the intermediate operation, the contact between the object and the sense organ is called "perception" (*pratyakṣa*). However, in some cases, it is [so called] with an intention to emphasize the substratum (*dharmin*).

A sense organ that is in contact with its own respective object is called perception (*pratyakṣa*). It is divided into the perception of the Lord (*īśvara*), the perception of Lakṣmī, the perception of the yogin, and the perception of the non-yogin. Among these, the first two consist solely of the nature of their own forms as sense organs; the latter two, however, consist of both types of sense organs [the physical and the mental]. As for the object:
It should be distinguished as being like the objects of those respective cognitions.

The classification of external sense organs is threefold: divine, demonic, and intermediate. Among these, that which abounds in knowledge of things as they truly are is divine; that which abounds in knowledge contrary to reality is demonic.

However, for those of middling capacity, the means of cognition is conceptual knowledge (*samajñāna*). Furthermore, even for those of superior capacity, their own sensory faculties are indeed accurate regarding both the essential nature and the specific mode of the object; yet for those of inferior and middling capacity, they are accurate only regarding the essential nature, while regarding the specific mode, they are inaccurate and confused.
Some maintain that the contact between the sense organ and its object is the cause of perceptual knowledge, and that this contact is divided into six types.

They are as follows: conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), inherence in what is inherent in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), inherence (*samavāya*), inherence in the inherent (*samavetasamavāya*), and the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). Among these:

There is a conjunction of the eye and the sense of touch with substances such as a jar, and of the mind with the self. There is a conjunct-inherent relation (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) of these [senses] with the qualities, actions, and universals residing in their own respective objects. Likewise, there is [a conjunct-inherent relation] of the nose and the tongue with odor and taste, and of these [two senses] with the universals residing in the qualities and actions of their own respective objects.
Conjunction-cum-inherence (saṃyukta-samaveta-samavāya);
the inherence of the auditory organ with sound; the inherence-in-what-is-inherent (samaveta-samavāya) with the universals residing therein;
and the relation of these five kinds of relations to the objects of non-existence (abhāva) and inherence (samavāya).

The claim that "the relationship between qualifier and qualified is fivefold" is incorrect. This is because qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth do not possess inherence (*samavāya*) with their substrates (*guṇin*) and so forth, due to their non-difference [from them]. Furthermore, the Self (*ātman*) and its attributes (*dharma*) are objects of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) and are not objects of the mind (*manas*). As for sound consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*), [it is likewise not an object of the mind].
Because it lacks the status of being a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of space as a substance (*dravya*). Therefore, for all the sense organs,
there is a direct contact with their respective objects and with the absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is their respective object, by means of the rays themselves.
Regarding the two-fold nature of perception:
they declare that perception is of two kinds, distinguished as non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*).
Among these, the non-conceptual is that which manifests the mere essential nature of the object; the conceptual has for its object a qualified form.
It is conceptual (savikalpaka). It is of eight kinds. Among these, the conceptualization of substance is, for example, "one with a staff" (daṇḍī).
The conceptualization of quality is, for example, "white" (śukla). The conceptualization of action is, for example, "he goes" (gacchati).
The conceptualization of genus is, for example, "cow" (gauḥ). The conceptualization of particularity is, for example, "distinguished" (viśiṣṭaḥ).
"An atom," for example; "a conceptualization of inherence," such as "the threads possess the cloth through inherence";

"a conceptualization of a name," such as "Devadatta"; and "a conceptualization of non-existence," such as "the ground possesses the absence of a jar. This too is incorrect, because particularity (*viśeṣa*) and inherence (*samavāya*) lack any basis in valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*), and [the same applies to] names.

Furthermore, since the cognition of non-existence depends upon the recollection of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), its conceptualization cannot arise immediately after the first sensory contact; yet, as there is no obstacle to the conceptualizations of substances and so forth arising at that very first moment, the existence of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) is untenable.

Some say that the result of perception consists of the cognitions of avoidance, acquisition, or indifference; however, that too is incorrect, because those [cognitions] are actually the results of inference. For instance, having merely presented the nature of a thorn or similar object...

Direct perception ceases [its operation]. Now, having remembered that a previously experienced object such as a thorn was a means to an undesirable end, and inferring that this present object is likewise a thorn, the cognition of avoidance (*hāna-buddhi*) arises. Similarly, regarding a plantain fruit and the like, after inferring its status as a means to a desirable end, the cognition of acquisition (*upādāna-buddhi*) arises. And regarding grass and such things, having inferred indifference, the cognition of equanimity (*upekṣā-buddhi*) is attained.
Therefore, the result of direct perception is indeed the direct apprehension of a qualified object.
Thus ends the chapter on direct perception (*pratyakṣapariccheda*) in the *Pramāṇapaddhati* composed by the venerable and worshipful Jayatīrtha.
The section on inference:
the definition of inference.
Valid establishment (*upapatti*) is inference (*anumāna*). Establishment, the pervaded (*vyāpya*), reasoning (*yukti*), and the logical mark (*liṅga*) are synonyms.

Inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is pervasion (*vyāpti*); that is to say, it is the rule of concomitance (*sāhacarya-niyama*). The object of pervasion is the pervaded; its agent is the pervader. For example, smoke has an inseparable connection with fire.

The relationship [is established] by the rule: "Where there is smoke, there is fire. In that case, smoke is the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and fire is the pervader (*vyāpaka*). Indeed, the movement of properties is fourfold: some are co-extensive (*samavṛtti*), such as being prohibited and being a means to sin; where there is being prohibited, there is being a means to sin, and where...

In that context, being a means to evil is necessarily defined as being prohibited; thus, between these two, there is a mutual relationship of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*). Some [properties] have a range of occurrence that is either lesser or greater, such as the possession of smoke and the possession of fire. In that case, the possession of smoke, having a lesser range of occurrence, is exclusively the pervaded.

The state of possessing more extensive activity (*adhikavṛttyagnimatva*) is indeed the pervader (*vyāpaka*). Some [properties] exist through mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāreṇa*), such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and "horseness" (*aśvatva*). For where there is cowness, there is in no way horseness; and where there is horseness, there is in no way cowness.
Among these, there is no relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*), because of the very absence of a connection.
Some [properties], although co-extensive in some cases, exist in others through mutual exclusion, such as "being a cook" and "being a human. In the case of a particular person, these two...
Even when co-located, the property of being a cook exists among women while excluding manhood;

manhood also exists in a man who is not cooking while excluding the property of being a cook. These two, moreover, do not possess a relationship of mutual pervasion (vyāpyavyāpakabhāva), even though such a connection exists.

Because they are mutually deviant. In that context, the pervaded property (*vyāpyadharma*), being the means for establishing the cognition of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), is called inference (*anumāna*); and the pervader is the object of inference (*anumeya*).
Now, [one might ask: "Is not smoke existing on a mountain [known] to a person inside a house?"

Why does it not produce the valid cognition of fire? It is said: inference, unlike perception, does not function with respect to an unknown object; rather, [its object] must be correctly known. Even so, why is there no arising of the valid cognition of fire for an inhabitant of Nārikela-dvīpa who has traveled to another land when there is the cognition of smoke? It is said:
although he possesses knowledge of the nature of smoke, he lacks the knowledge that it is pervaded by fire.

Why is it that, even for one who knows the pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is sometimes no production of the valid cognition (*pramā*) of fire? Because of the absence of the recollection of the pervasion.

Why, for one who possesses the recollection of the pervasion and has seen smoke on a mountain, does the valid cognition of fire not arise with respect to something other than that mountain? [Because] the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) depends upon the specific mode of the pervasion.
Because there is a rule that [the knowledge of the mark] generates the knowledge of the probandum.
The varieties of pervasion (*vyāpti*) are as follows: for example, there is pervasion between two things that occupy the same place and time, such as taste with respect to color.
In some cases, there is [spatial proximity] despite being in different times, as in the case of smoke with fire;

in some cases, despite being in the same time, they are in different places, as in the case of the rising of Kṛttikā being proximate to the rising of Rohiṇī; and in some cases, they are in different places and different times, as in the case of the lower region.

[The relation] of a river's flood with rain in an upper region [is one of non-concomitance], because [the flood] is occasional while [the rain] is co-spatial; as is the case of falling with gravity. [The relation] of something that is occasional with something that is co-spatial and constant [is one of non-concomitance]; as is the case of corporeality with destruction.

[The coexistence] of something existing in a limited part with something existing pervasively, as in the case of conjunction [existing in a part] with substantiality [which exists everywhere in the substance];

or of something existing pervasively with something existing in a limited part, as in the case of color [existing everywhere in a substance] with conjunction [which exists only in a part]; or of two things existing in the same composite whole yet distinguished by different parts, as in the case of...

"Regarding the rising and falling [of the balance]," and so forth. Thus, it is stated that inference is the correct cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) accompanied by the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and its recollection;
or rather, it is that which, having correctly cognized the mark according to the mode of its pervasion, produces the valid cognition of the mark in a suitable place and so on. For this very reason:

Even though the nature of the *liṅga* (the probans) is already known, inference is not rendered useless because it functions as a means of cognition by way of its connection with a specific location and so forth. Consequently, inference possesses a twofold capacity: pervasion (*vyāpti*) and establishment in a suitable location and so on. It is not, however, [merely the former].

The restriction of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Now, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) produced? It is produced, as the case may be, by perception, inference, and scripture.
We reply: First of all, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of smoke by fire is cognizable through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). To explain:
when a person observes the concomitance (*sāhacarya*) of smoke and fire in a kitchen or similar place, this reflection arises in him:
"Are these two, smoke and fire, concomitant only here, or [also] in another place and at another time?"

Furthermore, do these two things of this kind exist by mutually excluding one another, or does only one exist by excluding the other, or rather, are they always co-present throughout all space and time? Then, repeatedly seeing smoke, he sees fire;
and in the absence of fire, he sees the absence of smoke. Likewise...

Even in the absence of smoke, fire may exist in some places; therefore, the investigation proceeds once again. Just as fire, though accompanied by smoke in many instances, exists in some cases even while abandoning it, so too smoke, though existing together with fire in the places familiar to me, [may not do so elsewhere].
In some cases it occurs having abandoned that [property]; or does it always occur as its concomitant?
From this, the following thought arises: in the case of the connection between fire and smoke, there exists the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of conjunction with moist fuel;
and that [condition] pervades the smoke. When it itself is excluded, it [excludes the fire].
[He] has turned [the argument] back. Not [can one say] fire does not [exist] again; because that [fire] would not be pervasive [of smoke].

Likewise, if there were some *upādhi* (limiting condition) in the connection of smoke with fire, then that too would deviate from fire. But if there is none, then because the connection is causeless, it constitutes the very nature (*svabhāva*) of smoke.
Having determined that its absence will not occur anywhere, one proceeds to search for a limiting condition (*upādhi*) in places such as a kitchen.
Among those [conditions], some properties are pervaders of both; for example, knowability (*prameyatva*). This [knowability] does not relate to this [connection].
Some are incapable of disrupting [the relation]. Some do not pervade both; for example, "being a kitchen" (*mahānasatva*).
Even these are not capable of disrupting this connection. Some pervade smoke but do not pervade fire;
for example, "conjunction with moist fuel" (*ārdrendhana-saṃyoga*). Although these are capable of separating smoke from fire, they are not [capable of disrupting the essential relation].

Regarding the separation of smoke from fire: that which is a pervader of fire but not a pervader of smoke, by withdrawing itself, would be able to disrupt this connection; however, such a thing simply does not exist, because it is not perceived. Even if it were beyond the senses, it would have to be known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and yet, it is not.
That [invariable concomitance] is apprehended through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, that which lacks a basis in valid knowledge does not even admit of doubt.
Therefore, for one who has determined that no limiting condition (*upādhi*) exists here, the cognition of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) arises.
[Objection: If this is so, then perception (*pratyakṣa*) would not be the grasper of pervasion (*vyāpti*). [Reply: Not so; because—

For perception, which grasps concomitance (*sāhacarya*), the auxiliary factors are repeated observation, the non-observation of deviation, and the ascertainment of the absence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*). Nor does the presence of different auxiliaries constitute a difference in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as is the case with recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
How can perception, which grasps only that which is present and proximate, [establish] pervasion (*vyāpti*) whose locus is the past and so forth?

If it is argued that [the cognition] should be grasped [as valid], we say no; for it is frequently observed that through the power of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), a new capacity manifests within the instruments of cognition (*karaṇa*).
Furthermore, when the natural connection of perceived smoke with fire has been ascertained, [it is established].

If smoke were to exist elsewhere as well, then the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) would occur in that case too, thinking "it is likewise for that [too]"; therefore, what inconsistency is there here? By this, the objection that one who apprehends the pervasion between cognisability (*prameyatva*) and nameability (*abhidheyatva*) would necessarily be omniscient is also refuted. Why?

If it is argued that all this is merely conceptualized, [we reply: it is precisely because of the observation of the effect. For instance, there is indeed the cognition of fire immediately following the observation of smoke, and that is not incorrect, because it is corroborated. Nor is the cognition of one thing based on the observation of another thing without a cause.

It must be so, for otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And since there is no other cause apart from the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the cognition of the suitability of the place, it is this very effect that leads one to postulate [the cause]. Just as, indeed, even when [a cause] is not perceived in a fragment of stone and the like—

One postulates the seed’s potency—which arises from auxiliary factors such as earth, water, and so forth—based on the observation of the sprout. As for the pervasion (vyāpti) that is to be known through inference, we shall illustrate it later.
Furthermore, there is no infinite regress regarding that inference’s dependence on pervasion, because [the series] ultimately terminates.

Because it is rooted in perception and scripture: the universal concomitance (vyāpti) in such cases as "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed" and "A cow must not be touched with the foot" is to be understood through scripture. Furthermore, there is no minor obstacle here, nor is there any dependence upon an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta).
The threefold nature of inference:

inference is of three kinds—namely, inference from effect, inference from cause, and inference from that which is neither effect nor cause. Among these, the first is, for example: smoke [is the mark] of fire. The second is, for example: [the rising of the moon].

The rising of a distinguished cloud is [the mark] for rain. However, this is the distinction: the effect merely allows one to infer the cause; but the cause, when complete, [allows one to infer] the effect. An example of the third [type] is: "taste [is the mark] of color. Furthermore, it is of two kinds: the perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) and the general (*sāmānyato*).

And "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) means: among those, that which infers an object suitable for perception is the "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), such as smoke [inferring] fire. That which infers an object not suitable for perception is the "generally seen" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), such as the cognition of color and so forth [inferring] the eye and so forth. Alternatively, it is the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between two things exactly as they are.
The relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) is observed when they are exactly as they are, such as in the case of smoke and fire.

Even though the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) may be of a different nature, when the relationship between the mark and the bearer of the mark is established through the persistence of their common form, it is "observed in general" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), as in the case of a farmer.

The inference that sacrifices and the like have results such as heaven is based on observing that activities such as plowing result in fruits such as grain; this is because there is a commonality of being the activity of a discerning person and having a fruit. Furthermore, inference is of two kinds.

Furthermore, it is of two kinds: inference as proof (*sādhana-anumāna*) and inference as refutation (*dūṣaṇa-anumāna*). Of these, the first is, for example, the means of proving fire through the cognition of smoke. Inference as refutation is also twofold:
the means of proving a faulty cognition (*duṣṭi-pramiti-sādhana*) and *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum). Of these, the first is, for example, "This is not..."
It is capable of establishing its own probandum. "Because it is sublated by valid cognition," and so forth.

*Tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) is the deduction of another fact upon the acceptance of some property. It has five constituent parts: the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the *āpādaka* (the antecedent condition) by the *āpādya* (the consequent), and its non-frustration by a counter-reductio (*pratitarka*).

The undesirable nature of what is to be avoided (āpādya) is twofold: the abandonment of what is established by valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇika-hāna) and the postulation of what is not so established (aprāmāṇika-kalpana).
Of these, the first is threefold, distinguished by the abandonment of what is perceived, what is inferred, and what is heard from scripture.
The second is also threefold, distinguished by the postulation of what is unperceived, what is uninferred, and what is unheard from scripture.

This very [consequence] is called "conceptual complexity" (*kalpanā-gaurava*) when multiple conceptualizations are required. It consists of the reduction of the consequence to its opposite and the fact that it is not favorable to the opponent. Furthermore, the undesirable consequence (*āpādya*) is divided into five types:
self-dependence (*ātmāśrayatva*), mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*), circular dependence (*cakrakāśrayatva*), infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and...

And [the term] "only undesirable" (*kevalāniṣṭam*). Due to its divisions, the *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) that takes the form of bringing about the acceptance of a term is also fivefold. Among these, for the sake of the production or cognition of that very [term], if one accepts the requirement for the production or cognition of it, the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśrayatva*)—in the form of being prior to itself—is brought about. If this jar... of this very [jar]...

If the producer of a jar were to exist, it would necessarily be prior even to itself. For whatever is the cause of something is observed to be prior to that thing; for example, the threads are the cause of a cloth and are prior with respect to it. Furthermore, there is no counter-argument here. If the jar itself were [the cause] of the jar...

If it were not the cause, then this undesirable consequence would follow; for this is indeed undesirable, because its existence prior to itself is unproven, and because it is improper to accept what is contradictory.
For existence prior [to something] means existing at a time when that thing is absent; and [the effect] does not exist at a time when its own absence is present.

It is not contradictory that it exists by itself. If its prior existence is not admitted, then it cannot be its own cause; nor can one thing be established as the producer of another in such a manner—these are the five limbs [of the argument]. Thus, regarding cognition as well, the cognition of that [object] with respect to the cognition of that [same object]...

Prior existence is what must be established. If one accepts that two things are causes for one another, then mutual dependence—characterized by prior existence relative to each other—is what results as a logical fallacy. If one accepts a causal relationship among many things like a wheel, then circularity—characterized by prior existence—is the resulting fallacy.

In the case of dependence on a cause that is neither established nor stable, there arises an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), characterized by the destruction of the perceived effect—which is another name for the "destruction of the root" (*mūlakṣaya*).
Furthermore, the mere production of an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*) is also threefold, according to the distinctions of producing the loss of what is seen, inferred, or heard;
and according to the distinctions of producing the postulation of what is unseen, un-inferred, or unheard. This same [distinction applies] when there is a multiplicity of things to be postulated.

This is called the "burden of conceptual construction" (*kalpanā-gaurava*). An example of the "abandonment of what is observed" (*dṛṣṭa-hāna*) is as follows: "If the mountain were without fire, then it would be without smoke. In this manner, other examples should also be sought in the treatises. Furthermore, even though *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) is a form of inference, the non-establishment of the *apādaka* (the antecedent condition) is not a fault.
Because in that case, the meaning of the term "establishment" (siddhi) consists merely in the acceptance by the opponent.

Thus, the contradiction with a means of valid cognition (pramāṇavirodha) and the departure from a tenet (apasiddhānta) regarding the consequence to be established (āpādya) are not defects, because [the consequence] "it becomes smokeless" is not a proof (asādhana). Just as in an inferential proof (sādhanānumāna), there is neither mere pervasion (vyāptimātra) nor the subject (pakṣa).

The means of establishing the proof of the probandum is merely the nature of things (*dharmatā*), yet it is only when combined [with other factors] that it functions as such. Thus, both the production of an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*) and its culmination in the opposite case (*viparyaye paryavasāna*) together constitute the means of inference; therefore, the validity of *tarka* (reasoning) is established. This very [reasoning], in some cases, operates by way of dispelling contrary doubts.
It also serves as an auxiliary to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the refutation of the opposing view:
some maintain that inference is of three kinds, distinguished as purely positive (*kevalānvayi*), purely negative (*kevalavyatireki*), and positive-negative (*anvayavyatireki*).

The subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is the *pakṣa*. Therein, a subject that possesses a property identical to the proven property and is ascertained to exist through pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the *sapakṣa*. That which exists in all or in a part of it [the *sapakṣa*] is [the valid reason]. A subject devoid of the property to be proven and its similar properties is the *vipakṣa*. That which is devoid of that [the *vipakṣa*] is the purely positive (*kevalānvayi*).
It is of two kinds, due to the distinction between existing in all *sapakṣas* or in a part of them. For example: "Sound is denotable."

"Because it is cognizable" (*prameyatvāt*) is a reason that pervades the similar instances (*sapakṣavyāpaka*), because cognizability exists in everything that is generally agreed upon as being denotable. "Because it is a quality" (*guṇatvāt*) is a reason that occurs in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣaikadeśavṛtti*), because it exists in [qualities] such as color (*rūpa*) but does not exist in [substances] such as a jar (*ghaṭa*).

It is said that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is of two kinds: by positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and by negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Positive concomitance is the pervasion of the probans (*sādhana*) by the probandum (*sādhya*); negative concomitance is the pervasion of the absence of the probandum by the absence of the probans. In this case, there exists only positive concomitance: "Whatever is knowable is expressible, just like a pot. There is no [negative concomitance].

In this regard, there is no negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), because there is no instance [of something] that is not denotable and yet is not cognizable; for since everything is denotable, there is no possibility of anything being non-denotable.
Therefore, this is called a purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) [reason].

A *kevalavyatirekin* (purely negative) reason is that which pervades the subject (*pakṣavyāpaka*), lacks a similar instance (*avidyamānasapakṣa*), and is excluded from all dissimilar instances (*sarvasmādvipakṣād vyāvṛtta*). For example: "The class of living bodies possesses a self, because they possess breath and so forth. For this [reason], there exists only a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): namely, "whatever does not possess a self does not possess breath and so forth," as in the case of a jar. However, [there is no positive concomitance].

The positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is: "Whatever possesses breath and so forth is endowed with a self (*sātmaka*)," because every living body constitutes the subject (*pakṣa*), while everything else is devoid of a self. Therefore, this [reason] is called a purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) one. A reason that pervades the subject, occurs in all similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and is excluded from all dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is called a positive-negative (*anvayavyatirekin*) one. That too—

It is of two kinds, based on the distinction between that which pervades the entire similar class (*sapakṣa*) and that which exists in only a portion of it. "Sound is impermanent because it is produced" is a reason that pervades the entire similar class, since the property of being produced exists in all things that are impermanent.
"The mountain possesses fire because it has smoke" is a reason that exists in only a portion of the similar class; for although it exists in some things possessing fire, it does not exist in others.

Because it exists in some cases and is absent in others. For this [reason], since there is the presence of both types of pervasion— namely, "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, as in a kitchen" (positive concomitance), and "whatever does not possess fire does not possess smoke, as in a lake" (negative concomitance)— it is called *anvaya-vyatirekin* (possessing positive and negative concomitance).
The claim that negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is useless is incorrect. This is because negative concomitance is indeed useful for establishing the probandum under discussion.
For when a positive entity is to be proven by means of another positive entity, the concomitance of an absence with an absence is not what is required.
Furthermore, if this were the case, there would be a lack of common locus (*vaiyyadhikaraṇya*) between the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

How, then, is the conventional usage of the "purely negative" (*kevalavyatirekin*) inference maintained in the treatises? It is as follows: even in that case, the pervasion is simply "whatever possesses breath and so forth is endowed with a self. However, [the difference lies in the following:]...

Since the very locus where pervasion (*vyāpti*) is grasped has become the object of dispute, that [pervasion] could not be demonstrated. Therefore, in order to establish it by means of inference, a negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is set forth. When the reason "because of possessing breath and so forth" (*prāṇādimattvāt*) is employed, how is this...?
When there is the expectation [of the question], "What is pervasion (vyāpti)?", it is the state of possessing breath and so forth that is pervaded by the state of having a self (sātmakatva).

This is because it is the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the absence of that [having a self]. Whatever is the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the absence of something else is pervaded by that thing; for example, the state of possessing smoke is pervaded by the state of possessing fire—this is the meaning.

Because it is what is intended to be expressed. In the case of an inference based on both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekin*), however, negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is entirely useless, since the intended pervasion is established by perception and other means. Or, it might be of some use insofar as it demonstrates the absence of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Furthermore, inference is of two kinds: for oneself (*svārtha*) and for others (*parārtha*). Among these, that which occurs by oneself, without depending on instruction from another, [consists of] the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) together with the recollection thereof.

The cognition of the logical mark (*liṅga*) that arises is inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*). However, that which arises depending upon the instruction of another is inference for others (*parārthānumāna*).
Because it generates that [inference], the instruction of another is also sometimes figuratively designated as "inference for others."

Regarding instruction for others, the Naiyāyikas and others maintain that it consists of five-membered statements. The members are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*). These same members are called by the Vaiśeṣikas the proposition (*pratijñā*), the instruction (*upadeśa*), the illustration (*nidarśana*), the connection (*anusandhāna*), and the restatement (*pratyāmnāya*). Among these:

The statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) is the declaration of the side [to be proven], such as "the mountain possesses fire. In that context, having first indicated the subject (*dharmin*), the property (*dharma*) must subsequently be predicated.
The reason (*hetu*) is the statement of the mark (*liṅga*) ending in a case-ending that expresses its status as a means of proof (*sādhanatva*). For example:
"Because it possesses smoke. The locus where the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). It is of two kinds:
the example by similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) and the example by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Among these, the locus where positive pervasion (*anvaya-vyāpti*) is apprehended is the example by similarity. This is the case, for instance, in the inference from smoke.

The kitchen is the locus for grasping negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*); it is the instance of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), as in that very same case, "the great lake. An example (*udāharaṇa*) is the statement of an instance preceded by the demonstration of correct pervasion (*vyāpti*). It is of two kinds: the example of similarity (*sādharmya-udāharaṇa*) and the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-udāharaṇa*). [The former] is preceded by the demonstration of positive pervasion (*anvaya-vyāpti*).

The statement of an example based on similarity is the *sādharmyodāharaṇa* (example by similarity). For instance: "Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, just as a kitchen. The statement of an example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*), preceded by the demonstration of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*), is [the *vaidharmyodāharaṇa*].

The example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyodāharaṇa*) is as follows: "Whatever is not possessed of fire is not possessed of smoke, such as a great lake. The application (*upanaya*) is the statement that the pervasion of the mark (*liṅga*), whose inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the probandum is well-established in the example, exists in the subject (*pakṣa*); it too is of two kinds, according to the type of example.

In that context, "the mountain is also smoky, like a kitchen" is the application by similarity (*sādharmyopanaya*). "And this mountain is not smokeless, like a lake" is the application by dissimilarity (*vaidharmyopanaya*). The restatement of the thesis together with its reason is the conclusion (*nigamana*), as in: "Therefore, the mountain possesses fire."

Regarding the refutation of the Bhaṭṭa and Buddhist positions: the Bhaṭṭas maintain that there are exactly three members [of a syllogism], namely the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*udāharaṇa*); or alternatively, they hold them to be five: the proposition, the reason, the example, the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*). The Buddhists, however, maintain that there are only two: the example and the application. This [view] is incorrect.

Since the twofold division of the example (*udāharaṇa*) and the application (*upanaya*) has also been refuted by the refutation of the twofold nature of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and because a restrictive rule [regarding these] is untenable; for this sentence does not, as a scripture (*āgama*),
convey the pervasion and so forth, such that a restriction to five members or the like would follow according to the requirements of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and the rest.

It may be so; for there is no certainty regarding the pervasion (vyāpti) of one thing by another. Or, if such certainty were already established, the mere statement of the proposition (pratijñā) would suffice, rendering the articulation of the reason (hetu) and other members superfluous. Rather, it is useful for a person who has already grasped the pervasion as a reminder of it, while for one who has not grasped the pervasion, it serves to generate the desire to know it.

Furthermore, this recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth is experienced by you in all four ways; so what is the use of this restriction? Other modes are also possible, such as: "The mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke, like a kitchen."

Either the statement of the subject containing the reason, such as "the smoky mountain possesses fire," or, when the proposition is established through debate, the mere reason—such as "because of its possession of smoke"—in response to the question, "How is it that the mountain possesses fire? or when asked, "What is the proof for the mountain's possession of fire? [the answer is given].

Either it is merely the statement of the mark (*liṅga*) as "possessing smoke"; or it is the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) together with the proposition (*pratijñā*) and containing the reason (*hetu*), such as "the mountain, like a kitchen possessing smoke, possesses fire"; or it is the application (*upanaya*) stating "smoke, which is pervaded by fire, exists here on this mountain"; or [the conclusion]: "therefore, because of its possessing smoke characterized by pervasion and so forth, the mountain possesses fire."
Or it is the conclusion (*nigamana*). All these types [of inference] are conventional (*sāṃvyāvahārika*) in all the treatises; such is the nature of inference.
Now, it has been stated that "inference is a faultless logical justification" (*nirdoṣopapatti*). What, then, are the faults of justification in this context?

Those defects are those which, when present, cause the cognition intended as a logical mark (*liṅga*) not to arise at all, or produce doubt or error. They are of two kinds, distinguished as defects of the object and defects of the statement.
Among these, contradiction (*virodha*) and lack of connection (*asaṅgati*) are defects belonging directly to the logical reason itself; by extension, they also belong to the statement.

The defects of expression (*vacanadoṣa*) consist in deficiency and excess. Through the medium of the words, there is also [defect] regarding the meaning. Among these, contradiction (*virodha*) is the absence of compatibility (*yogyatā*). Incoherence (*asaṅgati*) is the absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Deficiency (*nyūna*) is the statement of only a portion when something must necessarily be stated; it is a specific case of the absence of proximity (*sannidhi*). [It also occurs when] that which is expected has already had its purpose fulfilled by another.

Excess of speech (*vacanādhikya*). These various types of contradiction (*virodha*) and so forth are twofold: those common to the form of debate (*kathā*), which consists of the binding of rules, the posing of questions, the establishment of one's own position, and the refutation of the opponent's position; and those residing in inference (*anumāna*). Among these, those residing in inference are first stated. There are three kinds of contradiction in inference, distinguished by contradiction with the thesis (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Among these, there is contradiction with authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇavirodha*) and contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*).
Thus, contradiction of the thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*) is of two kinds. Contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavirodha*) is also twofold:

contradiction with a stronger means of valid cognition (*prabalapramāṇavirodha*) and contradiction with an equally strong means of valid cognition (*samabalapramāṇavirodha*). This is because that which is weaker, being sublated by this [stronger means], is ineffective. Furthermore, strength is twofold: by way of multiplicity...
And by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Intrinsic nature consists of such forms as being the basis of reliance (*upajīvyatva*) and being without scope (*niravakāśatva*).

Both [types of contradiction]—contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth—are each threefold according to their specific distinctions. Contradiction with an inference of equal strength (*samabala-anumāna-virodha*) is also twofold: by that very same inference and by another inference.

Contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) is also of two kinds: *apasiddhānta* (departure from a tenet) and *jāti* (futile rejoinder). Among these, *apasiddhānta* is the acceptance of something contrary to what was previously accepted by the ancient masters as authoritative; for even the word of an ancient master constitutes "one's own word" (*svavacana*) since it has been accepted by oneself.
The definition of *jāti* (self-stultification) is:

*jāti* is a contradiction within one's own statement. It is of three kinds: contradiction between two words or two subordinate sentences within a single sentence composed by the same author; contradiction with one's own action; and contradiction with one's own logic.

And there is contradiction (*virodha*). Contradiction of the reason (*hetu*) is also of two kinds: non-establishment (*asiddhi*) and non-pervasion (*avyāpti*). Non-establishment is the lack of valid cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) in the appropriate locus. Non-pervasion is threefold: [the mark’s] relation with the probandum (*sādhya*), its absence, and [finally] when there is no relation with the probandum, yet [there is a relation] with its absence.

The contradiction [of the reason] consists in the absence of that very [property] and the absence of the relation between both. Furthermore, the contradiction with the example is also twofold: deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) and deficiency in the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*). Contradiction with one’s own words regarding the reason and so forth is already subsumed under [the fallacy of] non-establishment (*asiddhi*) and the like.

It has not been stated. Likewise, inconsistencies, deficiencies, and redundancies are each threefold, according to the distinctions of the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). We shall demonstrate these examples, along with contradictions and other such points common to the form of discourse, by showing how they are included within these very categories of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) propounded by others.
Not only are the faults of proof subsumed under contradiction and so forth; what then?

All the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) formulated by the Naiyāyikas are included within these very two speaker-faults, namely, inconsistency (*saṃvāda*) and non-statement (*anukti*). Consequently, contradiction and incoherence—
Deficiency and excess are non-statement and contradiction; thus, there are only six points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

Contradiction (*saṃvāda*) is the acceptance of a thesis regarding an object of knowledge that has been contested. Non-statement (*anukti*) is the failure to state that which must necessarily be stated for the purpose of informing another.

In debate, when one opponent, with unbroken pride, breaks the pride of another, it is called defeat (*parājaya*) or a point of defeat (*nigraha*). The occasion for that is a "point of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*). And the breaking of pride is the failure of one's intention to establish one's own position and to refute the position of the opponent. For this very reason, [the following] are extraneous to the debate:

Even in the case of a discussion (*kathā*), those states such as epilepsy or insanity, which are immediately concealed by means of a formal agreement (*saṃvaraṇa*) so that there is no opportunity for their manifestation, as well as those that are manifest before one's eyes but are not relevant to the subject at hand or are brought forward by an unqualified person, are excluded. Ignorance regarding what has been stated by another or what one intends to say oneself, as well as erroneous knowledge, [are also excluded].
Or it is a defeat; or rather, a point of defeat is that which possesses those characteristics.
And these are: abandonment of the thesis, shifting the thesis, contradiction of the thesis, renouncing the thesis, shifting the reason, the irrelevant, the meaningless, and so forth.
Meaningless speech, irrelevant speech, mistimed speech, deficient speech, redundant speech, repetitive speech, failure to restate, lack of understanding,
lack of ingenuity, distraction, admission of one's own position, and neglecting to censure when one should.
There are twenty-two [points of defeat]: the charging of one who is not to be charged, the deviation from a tenet (*apasiddhānta*), and fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
Among these, "abandonment of the proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*) is the relinquishing of that very thing, in that same manner, and for that same purpose of being proven, as it was originally stated.

This is an abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*). For example, when it has been stated, "The mountain possesses fire because it is an object of cognition," and this reason is shown to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), one says, "In that case, let the mountain not possess fire. This, however, is merely a contradiction;
it is a shift to another thesis (*pratijñāntara*).

*Pratijñāntara* (a different proposition) is the addition of a further qualification to the part of the thesis (*sādhya*) that was initially stated without qualification. The "part of the thesis" consists of the proposition (*pratijñā*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), and the application (*prayojya*), as well as the conclusion (*nigamana*). For instance, when it has been proposed that "sound is impermanent," [and subsequently... by means of sounds...

Regarding the pointing out of the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*), such as [the argument] "sound, consisting of phonemes, is impermanent," the following must be asked: does the same debate continue, or is it a different debate? It cannot be the first, because a debate persists or terminates only upon the establishment or the refutation of a single means of proof (*sādhana*) or a means of disproof (*dūṣaṇa*).

Because it is already concluded; because the presentation of another proof would be redundant; and because this is not the same as what was stated previously—for if it were so, it would follow that it is already refuted by the previous critique. Nor is the second [alternative] the case; for if that were so, [the fault would have occurred] at the very first.

Because the qualified [subject] has already been accepted, there is no "shifting the proposition" (*pratijñāntara*). However, in a formal debate (*vāda*), even if the discussion remains the same, this is not a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), because one must continue to respond until the opponent's doubts are removed.
True; yet, even when both *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā* have ceased, for one who introduces a further qualification, [this constitutes a fault].
If it is asked, "What is the fault? we reply: "Incoherence and so forth. Even that is not a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), because it lies outside the scope of formal debate (*kathā*).
[Rather,] it is a contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*).

In a statement uttered by a single speaker, the mutual contradiction between its constituent words or intermediate sentences constitutes a "contradiction of the proposition" (*pratijñāvirodha*). For example: "My mother is barren," or "Substance is distinct from qualities because it is non-distinct [from them]. This is a contradiction of one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) precisely because it is the first type of such fallacy. This is the "abandonment of the proposition" (*pratijñāsaṃnyāsa*).
Renunciation of one's own proposition (*pratijñā-saṃnyāsa*) is the denial of what one has stated oneself. For example, when one has asserted,

"Fire is not hot," and a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa-virodha*) has been pointed out, if he then says, "I did not assert that fire is not hot," that too is indeed a contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-virodha*), because the statement itself was established as valid.
*Hetvantara* (a different reason) is the addition of something further to the probative portion (*sādhakāṃśa*) when it has already been stated as qualified by the first [reason].

The probative portion consists of the reason (*hetu*), the application (*upanaya*)—which is the factor that connects [the example] in the illustration (*udāharaṇa*)—and the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). For example:

When it is stated that "sound is eternal because it is perceptible by the senses," and the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) is raised on the basis of the universal (*sāmānya*), [the opponent] replies with "provided it possesses a universal" (*sāmānyavattve sati*), and so forth. This is refuted by the very refutation of the alternative proposition (*pratijñāntara*). Furthermore, since the mention of the "proposition" (*pratijñā*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of what has been stated, it should not be mentioned separately. If it were not intended as an illustration, then other examples and so forth would also have to be stated separately. By the term "proposition," the element of the probandum (*sādhya*)—

If it is argued that [the distinction] is thus indicated, we say no; for it would be redundant. Otherwise, why would a distinction not also be made in cases such as the abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*)?
[To do so would result in] an irrelevant subject matter (*arthāntara*).

The statement of something irrelevant to the subject at hand is the fallacy of "Irrelevance" (*arthāntara*). For example, in the argument "Sound is eternal because it is knowable," "knowability" is the reason (*hetu*). Furthermore, regarding the word "reason" (*hetu*), when the suffix *tu* is added to the root *hi*, the resulting form is a nominal base ending in a *kṛt* suffix, and so forth.
This is indeed an inconsistency because it is undesired.
"Meaningless" refers to the employment of words that lack expressive power; for example: "Sound is eternal, kacaṭatapānām."
"Jabagaḍadaṭakādityādi" and so forth. This, however, is simply a non-statement (*ananubhāṣaṇa*).
"Of unknown meaning" (*avijñātārtha*):
even when stated three times, if there is a word whose meaning is not understood by either the assembly or the opponent, that is "of unknown meaning."
