For example: "This [person] is endowed with a name identical to that of the son of the Three-Eyed One (Śiva), who is the cause of the stability of Kaśyapa’s daughter (Pārvatī)," and so forth;
or, "He possesses a banner like his," and so forth. This too is merely a non-statement (*anukti*);
it is incoherent (*apārthaka*).

The use of words that are either unconnected or non-expressive constitutes the "meaningless" (apārthaka). For example: "A bowl, a goat-skin, ten pomegranates, six cakes," and so forth. This is clearly incoherent.
[The next type is] the "untimely" (aprāptakāla).
The reversal of the proper order is an "inopportune time" (aprāptakāla). For example: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced," and so forth.

This is not in itself a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna), because there is meaningful practical usage, such as the statement: "A means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is purposeful because it possesses causal efficacy. However, a point of defeat consists precisely in a lack of logical connection (asaṅgati). [An example of] deficiency (nyūna) is as follows:
The omission of any one of the necessary [members] constitutes a deficiency (*nyūna*). For example: "The mountain possesses fire, like a kitchen," and so forth.
This is indeed a deficiency.
An excess (*adhika*) [is as follows:]...

The employment of what is redundant, what is superfluous, what is repetitive, or what has already been accomplished is "excessive" (*adhika*). For example: "The mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke and because it possesses a particular kind of light," and so forth. This is indeed excessive;
it is also [a form of] repetition.

Furthermore, the restatement of a meaning already understood by means of one's own words, without a specific purpose, is a tautology (*punarukta*). For example: "The mountain has fire; the mountain has fire," and so forth. This is indeed a superfluous addition. [Next is] non-reproduction (*ananubhāṣaṇa*).

When the meaning of what has been stated by the proponent has been understood by the judges, and that which is fit for repetition has been restated by either the proponent or the assembly, the failure to repeat it— without revealing one's own ignorance and without interrupting the discourse— is *ananubhāṣaṇa* (non-reproduction). It is of five kinds.

The restatement beginning with "that which... is a restatement of only a portion of the object to be refuted; mere statement of the refutation is a restatement otherwise; and silence is [another type]. Among these, the first three are deficient; the fourth is irrelevant; the fifth is non-statement; and ignorance is [the sixth].
Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the failure to comprehend the meaning of a statement that has been uttered three times by the proponent and understood by the assembly.
Lack of presence of mind (*apratibhā*) is the failure to provide a reply to what has been stated by the proponent.

Deflection (*vikṣepa*) is the interruption of a discourse under some pretext. For example, having begun a story, one says: "I have an important matter to attend to today; when that is finished, I shall speak. This is merely a failure to state [the intended point].

*Matānujñā* (admission of the opponent's position) is the acceptance of what is desired [by the opponent]. For example, when someone has admitted their own status as a thief and is told, "You are a thief because you are a human being," they reply, "In that case, the consequence of being a thief would also apply to you. This is merely an inconsistency (*asaṅgati*).
Overlooking the censurable (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*) is the failure to point out a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) that has been reached as something that must necessarily be pointed out;
this too is included within "non-statement" (*anukti*).

*Ananuyojyānuyoga* (the charge against one who is not to be charged) is the pointing out of a defeat (*nigraha*) where that defeat has not been incurred. It is fourfold: quibble (*chala*), futile rejoinder (*jāti*), fallacies such as "loss" (*hāni*) and so forth, and taking up [an objection] at an inappropriate time.

Quibble (*chala*) is the refutation of another's statement by imagining a different meaning for what was intended and then criticizing that [imagined] meaning. For example, when one says "Bring the cow" with the intention of referring to a young cow (*gṛṣṭi*), [the opponent might object].

"The bringing of a cow is impossible if one intends to speak of the earth"—this is inconsistent. For it is precisely the intended refutation that is required; since a refutation is possible even for a statement involving quibble (*chala*) by imagining a different meaning and claiming that "the bringing of a cow" is incoherent, this [objection] falls within the category of "contradiction of one's own logic" (*svanyāyavirodha*).
Quibble (*chala*). A futile rejoinder (*jāti*) is a reply capable of refuting even that which is established. And this incapacity is of two kinds.

It is both common and uncommon. Among these, the common [fallacy] is self-contradiction (*svavyāhati*), while the uncommon consists of the deficiency of necessary members (*yuktāṅgahīnatva*), the addition of unnecessary members (*ayuktāṅgādhikatva*), and the occurrence outside the proper domain (*aviṣayavṛttitva*). Furthermore, that [uncommon fallacy] is twenty-fourfold, distinguished by: similarity (*sādharmya*), dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), augmentation (*utkarṣa*), diminution (*apakarṣa*), the eulogized (*varṇya*), the non-eulogized (*avarṇya*), the alternative (*vikalpa*), the attainment of the probandum (*sādhyaprāpti*), the non-attainment (*aprāpti*), the consequence (*prasaṅga*), the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*), the non-arising (*anutpatti*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), the point of dispute (*prakaraṇa*), the non-reason (*ahetu*), presumption (*arthāpatti*), non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*), proof (*upapatti*), perception (*upalabdhi*), non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), eternity (*nitya*), non-eternity (*anitya*), and the effect (*kārya*). Among these:

When a proponent has employed a reason for establishing a thesis, the opponent’s presentation of a counter-position by means of a counter-means of valid cognition (*pratipramāṇa*) that possesses a logical factor not accepted [by the proponent] is the fallacy of "balancing the counter-property" (*pratidharmasama*). This is manifold, being divided into fallacious perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) and so forth.
It is [also known as] "balancing through similarity" (*sādharmyasama*).
In that regard, the objection raised by means of an inference lacking pervasion (*vyāpti*) is of two kinds:

by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) and by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Among these, an opposition based on similarity is a refutation known as "balancing the similarity" (*sādharmyasama*). For example, if [it is argued]: "Because of its similarity to a kitchen..."

If it is accepted that the mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke, then why is it not also accepted that it lacks fire because it possesses substanceness, which is a property shared with a lake?
This is the "balancing the heterogeneity" (vaidharmyasama) sophistical refutation.

The "balancing by dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyasama*) is a refutation consisting in an objection based on dissimilarity. For example: "If it is claimed that the mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke—which is dissimilar to a lake—then why is it not also claimed that the mountain lacks fire because it is a mountain—which is dissimilar to a kitchen? In this case:
First, one should point out the absence of the constituent factor characterized by pervasion (*vyāpti*), and not the status of being a "fallacy" (*jāti*).
This is because it is impossible even now to know whether the opponent holds the view that there is no pervasion existing within their own mind.

However, when the opponent says, "Is it not mere similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) that is the effective cause [of proof], rather than pervasion? [then one may address the fallacy].
Then it must be said: "This being the case, this [reason] is not a prover, because it is countered by an opposing argument.

For even in your own inference, there is a contradiction due to the possibility of a counter-argument based on similarity or dissimilarity that lacks pervasion (*vyāpti*). And thus, in the case of the negation:
It is included within the third type of *jāti*, which consists of contradicting one's own reasoning.
*Utkarṣasama* (balancing by addition) occurs when,
by the force of the proponent's argument, some undesirable property [is attributed] to the subject, even in the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*), just as the probandum [is established].

*Utkarṣasama* (balancing the addition) is the addition of a property to the subject (*pakṣa*) on the basis of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). For instance: "If the mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke, like a kitchen hearth, then for that very same reason, it must also possess pots and the like, just as the hearth does.

To this, the reply should be stated: "This is a fallacy of reasoning (*tarkābhāsa*) due to a deficiency in pervasion (*vyāpti*). For one who argues that reasoning proceeds by mere concomitance (*sāhacarya*) alone and asks what pervasion is for, there is a contradiction with his own logic (*svanyāyavirodha*), which constitutes a refutation (*vyāghāta*).

*Apakarṣasama* (balancing by subtraction) is, according to some, the subtraction of a property desired [in the thesis] from the subject and so forth; for example, when it is stated that "sound is non-eternal because it is produced," [the opponent objects]: "In that case, for that very same reason, sound should likewise not be audible."

Here it must be asked: is this a proof (*sādhana*) or a refutation (*apādana*)? It cannot be the first, because since it is a different matter (*arthāntara*), it does not constitute a "rejoinder against one who is not to be censured" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*). In the second case, however, this is simply the "balancing by superiority" (*utkarṣasama*). For no distinction is possible merely on the grounds that the superiority of an existence is not the superiority of a non-existence. Udayana, however, [says...]

He states that *apakarṣasama* (the "balancing by subtraction") consists in proving the absence of either of those two [the probandum or the probans] in the subject (*pakṣa*) through the exclusion of some property that is concomitant with the probandum or the probans in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). For example,

since the presence of a cooking pot and so forth— which is observed in a kitchen together with the possession of fire or the possession of smoke— is absent on the mountain, there must be an absence of both of those as well.

In that case, when proving the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), one would have to impute either "counter-balanced opposition" (*satpratipakṣatva*) or "sublation" (*bādha*); whereas when proving the absence of the probans (*sādhanābhāva*), one would have to impute "unestablishedness" (*asiddhi*). This too is incorrect, because it would result in the loss of distinction from the fallacies of "balancing the homogeneity" (*sādharmyasama*) and "balancing the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*) when proving the absence of the probandum. Therefore, [this objection] disregards pervasion (*vyāpti*).

The *apakarṣasama* (balancing by subtraction) consists precisely in establishing the absence of the probans (*sādhana*) in the subject (*pakṣa*). To this, the following response should be stated: there is an absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and there is no contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the probans. Furthermore, against one who asserts that mere concomitance (*sāhacarya*) alone is the determinant factor, rather than pervasion and so forth, the charge of "contradiction with one's own logic" (*svanyāyavirodha*) should be raised.
Some maintain that *varṇyasama* (balancing the subject) is the objection that the example is itself yet to be proven, just like the thesis (*pakṣa*). That is incorrect;
for an objection based on a disagreement regarding the probandum and the probans within the example constitutes a valid response. It is exactly thus.

Because such an objection is baseless and impossible to maintain; likewise, by that same reason, an objection regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) is also baseless. If an objection is raised on the grounds that the reason, having been observed in the subject (*pakṣa*) as concomitant with the probandum, must also establish it for the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), this is precisely the "balancing the addition" (*utkarṣasama*) fallacy. In the case of the subject...

If the objection is that there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because of the mere difference consisting in the "excess" (*utkarṣaṇa*) found in the example, then there would be no distinction from the "equal to the probandum" (*sādhyasama*). Therefore, Udayana maintains that *varṇyasama* consists in attributing the status of being a "probandum" (*sādhyatva*) to the example by means of its possessing or lacking a reason (*hetu*) characterized by such features as having an unestablished object (*asiddhārthatva*) which is intended for the subject (*pakṣa*) alone; for instance, if smoke-possessingness (*dhūmavattva*), which is unestablished [in the subject], exists in the kitchen just as it does on the mountain, then that [kitchen] too [would be a probandum].
The subject would have to be established as possessing the probandum; otherwise, it would not be established as possessing the means of proof.

Here too, one should not say that the consideration of specific characteristics is useless since the status of being an example is established by the mere existence of the nature of the reason (*hetu*). For, even if one accepts that such [specificity] is necessary...
Regarding "contradiction with one's own reasoning":

some maintain that *avarṇyasama* (the "equal to the unprovable") is the objection that the subject (*pakṣa*), like the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), is itself not something to be proven. In this case as well—

Furthermore, an objection raised with the conceit that [the probandum] is already established is not a valid rejoinder; otherwise, it would be groundless (*nirbīja*). However, if the objection is raised by the force of the concomitance (*sāhacarya*) with the proof, it is simply the "balancing the excellence" (*utkarṣasama*) fallacy. Therefore, Udayana maintains that *avarṇyasama* is the objection that the subject (*pakṣa*) is not the thing to be proved, based on the presence or absence of a reason possessing the form of having a purpose already established and so forth, as found in the mere example (*dṛṣṭānta*). For instance, regarding a purpose already established...

If the presence of smoke exists on the mountain just as it does in the kitchen, then because the probandum is already established, there is no longer a probandum; if it does not exist there, then because of the absence of a means [to establish it], there is no probandum. The inclusion of this [fallacy] within the previous one must also be stated.
This is *vikalpasama* (balancing the alternative).

The "balancing by alternative" (vikalpasama) consists in urging that the probans (*sādhana*) is also subject to deviation from the probandum (*sādhya*), by pointing out the observation of deviation between one property and another among phenomena (*dharma*). For example, although there is no difference in their being produced (*kṛtakatva*), some things such as a jar are seen to be corporeal (*mūrta*), while others such as form (*rūpa*) are incorporeal (*amūrta*); likewise [the case in question].

"Could it not be that some created thing is eternal and some is non-eternal? If this is merely a doubt, then it is indeed a valid response; it should be resolved by means such as the absence of a cause [for change]. If, however, one seeks to prove the deviation of this [property] through the deviation of another property, then that deviation of another property must be either the logical reason (*hetu*) or the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
In the first case, a lack of pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be stated. In the second, the argument is deficient due to the absence of a reason (*hetu*).

If one accepts the reason as a constituent part of the argument despite it not being a constituent part, there is a confusion with the fallacy of "the equal to the counter-example" (*pratidṛṣṭāntasama*).

If one accepts [the reason] as a property (*dharma*) and so forth as a constituent part, there is simply a lack of pervasion. However, if one does not accept that, there is a contradiction with one's own logic.

Some maintain that *sādhyasama* (the "equal-to-the-probandum") is the objection that the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is itself yet to be proven because it shares the nature of the probandum (*sādhya*). This is incorrect;
for such an objection based on a disagreement [with the opponent] would constitute a valid response (*saduttara*), and an objection made in this very manner would be logically impossible.

For that very reason, even when [the probandum] is reduced to the status of being the thing to be proven (*sādhya*), it is exactly the same. However, in the case of establishing the "equal-to-the-describable" (*varṇyasama*) fallacy, there is no such distinction. Therefore, since the logical mark (*liṅga*)—which has as its object the locus (*dharmin*) and so forth already subsumed within it—is ineffective with respect to the locus and so forth, by that same reason, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) follows that the probandum would likewise be ineffective.

Udayana maintains that *sādhyasama* (the "equal-to-the-probandum") consists in the reduction of even the property-possessor (*dharmin*) and so forth to the status of the probandum (*sādhya*). Since the probans is established as a member of the proof solely by virtue of its possessing the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and its invariable concomitance (*vyāpti*), it is possible for it to function as a means of proof merely through its being established;
therefore, the response should be that the proof is carried out by that very same reason. However, if this is not accepted, there is a contradiction with one's own logic.
*Prāptisama* (the equalization by attainment) and *aprāptisama* (the equalization by non-attainment):

*Prāptisama* is the subversion of the status of a means (*sādhana*) by refuting the position that it attains the probandum (*sādhya*). *Aprāptisama* is the subversion of that [status] by refuting the position of its non-attainment. This applies commonly to both production (*kṛti*) and manifestation (*jñapti*).

There are two possibilities. If the cognition of smoke produces the cognition of fire by means of reaching it (*prāpti*), then since that reaching must already exist, it cannot be the producer because it was already established prior to [the cognition]. Likewise, if the cognition of smoke makes fire known by reaching it, then, since no other form of reaching is possible, there would have to be a relationship of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) [between the two cognitions].

If it is argued that smoke does not possess the quality of being a cognizer (jñāpaka) of fire because fire is already manifest within the very cognition of smoke, this constitutes the "balancing the attainment" (prāptisama) fallacy. If it is claimed that being a cognizer consists in producing [cognition] without having reached [the object], that is not so; for such a thing is never observed anywhere.
Indeed, fire does not burn wood without reaching it, nor does a lamp illuminate what is to be illuminated without reaching it.

"Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)," [you argue,] thus making it a "balancing by non-attainment" (*aprāptisama*). To this, the reply should be stated as follows: in the case of *action* (*kṛti*), since there exists an attainment characterized by capacity (*sāmarthya*), there is no over-extension; therefore, attainment in the sense of essential nature (*svarūpa*) is simply not required. Even in the case of *cognition* (*jñapti*), since there exists an attainment consisting in the object being the domain of the probans that pervades it, there is no over-extension; therefore, the relation of subject and object (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) is simply not required. If one does not accept this and insists on the necessity of attainment in the sense of essential nature and so forth, then one contradicts one's own logic.

The "balancing by consequence" (*prasaṅgasama*) is the adducing of an appearance of infinite regress; it is called *prasaṅgasama* because it results in a consequence (*prasaṅga*). For example: "That which produces the mountain must be stated;
for that [producer] as well, [another producer] must be stated," and thus there is an infinite regress. Likewise, "that which makes the mountain known must be stated."

Regarding the phrase "there would be an infinite regress for that as well," it must be stated here that since there is the possibility of the [infinite series] coming to rest by taking a proven entity as its object, there is no fault because the root is not destroyed; however, if this is not accepted, it contradicts one's own logic.
This is the *pratidṛṣṭāntasama* (balancing the counter-example).

Some maintain that "balancing the counter-example" (*pratidṛṣṭāntasama*) is an objection based on a counter-example; however, that is incorrect, because such an objection occurs even in cases like "balancing the similarity" (*sādharmyasama*). For example, when it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," someone might say: "If it is impermanent due to being perceptible by the senses, as in the case of the example of a jar, then..."

If it is argued that there is no confusion with *sādharmyasama* (balancing the similarity) and other fallacies because this [fallacy] proceeds with the intention of urging a deviation (*vyabhicāra*)— asking "why should it not be eternal by way of a general example?"— we say no, because this is a false rejoinder (*asat-uttara*).
Therefore, the raising of either sublation (*bādha*) or counter-impediment (*pratirodha*) by means of a mere counter-example, independent of the reason (*hetu*), [constitutes the fallacy].

Udayana [calls this] "balancing the counter-example" (*pratidṛṣṭāntasama*). For example: "If [the mountain] is established as possessing fire by means of the kitchen as a supporting instance (*dṛṣṭānta*), then let it be without fire by means of a lake as a supporting instance," and so forth. In this case, a deficiency (*nyūnatva*) must be pointed out;
however, if one falsely assumes that the logical reason (*hetu*) is not a constituent part [of the proof], there is a contradiction with one's own logic.
*Anutpattisama* (the equal by non-arising) is the pointing out of non-establishment due to the absence of the operation of the reason prior to the arising of the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth.
For example: "Prior to the arising of the mountain, the possession of smoke did not exist there."

"Partially unestablished" (*bhāgāsiddha*), and so forth. Here, it should not be argued that because that which has not yet arisen lacks the nature of a mountain (*parvatatva*) and thus lacks the status of being the subject (*pakṣatva*), the absence of [the reason] in that [subject] is not a fault. For if this were not the case, there would be a contradiction with one's own logical principles.
This is "balancing the doubt" (*saṃśayasama*).

*Saṃśayasama* (the equalizing by doubt) consists in inducing doubt through the mere presence of a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) and so forth, even when a cause for certain determination exists. For example: "If there is a certainty of the presence of fire because of the presence of smoke, then why should there not be doubt regarding that [fire] due to its being a substance (*dravyatva*), which is common to both a lake and a kitchen? In that case, it is only when [the common property] is accompanied by the absence of a determining factor [that doubt arises].
It might be argued that because common properties and the like are causes of doubt, there can be no doubt here due to the presence of a decisive factor (*nirṇāyaka*).
However, for one who asserts that a decisive factor is not an inhibitor of doubt, this contradicts their own logic.
This is the "equal-to-the-issue" (*prakaraṇasama*) fallacy.

Some maintain that *prakaraṇasama* (the "neutralized" fallacy) consists in countering an argument with a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*). For example, when it is stated, "Sound is non-eternal because it is produced," one might respond, "Sound is eternal because it is audible, like the nature of sound (*śabdatva*). In this case, if one falsely believes that the counter-inference possesses all its necessary components (*aṅgasākalya*), it is merely a valid rejoinder; otherwise, it is included within the category of *sādharmyasama* (balancing the homogeneity).
Therefore, Udayana maintains that *prakaraṇasama* is the urging of a sublation by means of a counter-argument possessing superior force.

This too is incorrect; for just as in the case of *pratidṛṣṭāntasama* and others, they constitute a single class due to the urging of one or the other [alternative], so too since *sādharmyasama* and the rest could likewise belong to a single class, their separate classification would be untenable.
The refutation (*uddhāra*) is exactly as before.
*Ahetusama* (the "equal to a non-reason"):
the pointing out of the lack of causality by rejecting the prior, posterior, or simultaneous existence of the reason in relation to the probandum is *ahetusama*.

Just as the means of proof cannot exist prior to the probandum, because in the absence of a probandum it is impossible for something to be defined as a "means of proof"; nor can the means of proof exist posterior to the probandum, because in the absence of a means of proof there can be no connection with a probandum;
nor can the two exist simultaneously, because in that case there would be no distinction between them, making the relationship of probandum and means of proof untenable.

In this context, regarding the act (*kṛti*), that which exists prior [to the result] possesses the status of a means (*sādhana*). This is because the capacity of being a means does not depend on anything else, and its designation as such is established by the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) as it exists in the mind. Regarding cognition (*jñapti*), however, all three positions apply according to the circumstances. The distinction between these cases should be stated as being due to the difference between being known and being unknown.
But if that is not accepted, there is a contradiction with one's own logic.
*Arthāpattisama* (the equalization by presumption) is an opposition based on a fallacious presumption (*arthāpattyābhāsa*). For example:

When it is stated that "the mountain possesses fire," it follows by implication that "something else does not possess fire," and so forth; thus, the example would be devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*). In this context, *arthāpatti* (presumption) is the cognition of a non-establishing factor based on the observation of something that is otherwise inexplicable. However, in this case, there is nothing whatsoever that is inexplicable; therefore, this is not [an instance of *arthāpatti*].

It should be stated that this is a *prasaṅga* (an undesirable consequence). However, if one accepts that *arthāpatti* (presumption) consists merely in the expectation of the opposite of what has been stated, then there would be a contradiction with one's own logic. This is not a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*) because it lacks the seed of the *upapattisama* (balancing the justification).
It is rather *aviśeṣasama* (balancing the non-distinction).

*Aviśeṣasama* (the equalization of non-distinction) is the application of a property other than the one under proof to all things possessing that [original] property, thereby resulting in their lack of distinction. For example: "If there is no distinction between the mountain and the kitchen in terms of possessing fire because both possess smoke, then it follows that there is no distinction among all entities in terms of impermanence because they all equally exist. To this, the response should be stated: "This is not a valid counter-argument (*prati-bandī*), because there is a distinction based on the presence or absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other such factors."
If one proceeds without accepting that [reason], there is a contradiction with one's own logic;
this is *upapattisama*.
Some say that *upapattisama* is an opposition based on the justification of both reasons. For example, if...

If it is argued that impermanence is accepted because sound possesses "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), which establishes its impermanence, then why is permanence not also accepted because sound possesses "intangibility" (*asparśatva*), which establishes its permanence?
This is incorrect, because it is not distinct from the fallacy of "balancing the homogeneity" (*sādharmya-sama*). Therefore, even in my own position, there is some means of proof.
Udayana maintains that "balancing the production" (*upapattisama*) is the general counter-argument stating, "it will come to be.

This too is incorrect; for liberation is seedless (*nirbīja*) only when considered in isolation. However, if it is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then if the establishing factor is sound, it is a valid rejoinder (*saduttara*); if it is unsound, then since that very defect must be pointed out, it does not constitute a futile rejoinder (*jāti*).
Regarding *upalabdhisama* (the equal by apprehension):

some maintain that it is the statement that a reason is irrelevant because the probandum is apprehended even in the absence of the stated reason. For example, [the claim that] the presence of fire is irrelevant [as a reason] because fire is apprehended in some places even in the absence of smoke.

Regarding the phrase "possessing smoke": since there is no seed for its [the opponent's] rise, this is not a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*); rather, it is merely a semblance of a defeat such as "loss" (*hāni*). Thus, Udayana maintains that *upalabdhisama* (balancing the perception) consists in superimposing an intention of restriction onto the disputant’s statement, and then offering a refutation by means of a dilemma regarding that restriction. For example, when it is said, "The mountain possesses fire," [one might ask]: what...

[The opponent argues: "Is it that 'the mountain alone possesses fire,' or that 'the mountain possesses fire alone'? The first [alternative] is not tenable, because the kitchen and so forth also possess fire. The second is not tenable, because at some time [the mountain] may lack fire," and so on. This too is incorrect, because it is a case of a general doubt (*sāmānyacala*) due to the superimposition of another intended meaning (*tātparya*). If it is argued that this is not so because it arises as a conceptual alternative (*vikalpa*), we say no; for the very function of the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*)...

Because there is no avoidance of the superimposition of restriction through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). If it is argued that for those who delight in the meaning of a sentence as an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), restriction is indeed established, we say no; for even they do not accept such a restriction, since they only admit the exclusion of what is other than that (*atad-vyāvṛtti*). This is the "equal to non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhisama*) fallacy.

*Upalabdhisama* (the "equalization by apprehension") consists in the production of a contradiction regarding the true nature of properties such as apprehension by means of their occurrence or non-occurrence within themselves. For example: if apprehension exists in itself, then because it is an apprehension, it would follow that it is non-apprehension, like a jar; if it does not exist in itself, then likewise it remains non-apprehension, and so forth. Here, one must state that the status of being an apprehension is not negated with respect to its object by its occurrence or non-occurrence within itself. If this is not accepted, there is either a contradiction with one's own logic or a contradiction with one's own action (*svakriyāvirodha*).

The "eternal" (nityasama) [futile rejoinder] consists in the subversion of a subject's being qualified by a property through the alternative of whether that property is eternal or non-eternal. For example, when it is stated that "sound is impermanent," one might ask: is impermanence eternal or non-eternal? In the first case...

In the first case, there would be the consequence of the subject (*dharmin*) being eternal; in the second, upon its destruction, there would again be the consequence of sound being eternal, and so forth. Here, if the intention is merely to point out the difficulties in the opponent's position while intending to provide a different way of accounting for one's own position, then it is indeed a valid rejoinder (*saduttara*). However, if it is intended to refute the specific nature [of the opponent's view], then one must first state the way of accounting for one's own position.
For one who proceeds without accepting that [distinction], there is a contradiction with one's own logic and one's own action.

*Anityasama* (the "equal to the impermanent") is the application of the property of being the probandum to those who state a counter-argument by means of another property, through a refutation of the proponent's proof.
For example: "If sound were impermanent because it is produced, then everything would be impermanent because it exists.
This too, being subsumed by the very definition of *aviśeṣasama* (balancing the non-distinction), need not be mentioned separately.
[Next is] *kāryasama* (balancing the effect).

Some maintain that *kāryasama* (the "equal-to-the-effect" sophism) is an objection based on the doubt regarding the non-establishment of the reason (*hetu*). For example, when it is stated, "Sound is eternal because it follows immediately after effort," the reason—following immediately after effort—is doubted as to whether it is produced (*utpādyatva*) or manifested (*vyaṅgyatva*). This [objection] is also merely an exposure of the reason's being established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*).

It is precisely this: Udayana maintains that *kāryasama* (the "equal-to-the-effect" fallacy) consists in the defeat of the proponent’s proof by either pointing out the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of any one of the members of the syllogism, such as the thesis (*pakṣa*), or by refuting that which has been conceived by oneself as its establisher.
For example, when it is stated, "Sound is eternal because it is an effect," the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is unestablished; and that which establishes it—
Or, one might state that "being produced immediately after an effort" [is the definition]; yet that is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*).
This too is merely a quibble (*chala*), due to the imposition of an unintended intention.
This is the semblance of abandonment (*hāny-ābhāsa*).
Even when there is no actual loss of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*) or other such faults, the pointing out of them through error or the like constitutes a "semblance" (*ābhāsa*) of loss and so forth;

this is indeed a contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavirodha*), because the semblances of loss and so forth are recognized as such by the judges (*prāśnika*) and others. Their apprehension occurs at an inappropriate time.

To point out a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) when the time for pointing it out has not yet arrived, or to do so after that time has passed, is "taking [the opponent] at an inappropriate time" (*aprāptakāla*). That is indeed irrelevant; it is a "departure from a tenet" (*apasiddhānta*).

Deviation from a tenet (*apasiddhānta*), however, is simply a contradiction with one's own statement; for example, a follower of the Prabhākara school accepting the existence of God (*īśvara*). Fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are [to be understood as] fallacious reasons.

The five characteristics of a logical reason (*hetu*) are: presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), existence in the similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*), exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*), the state of having an uncontradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), and the absence of a counter-balancing argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*). Among these, all five are intended for a reason that possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekin*).

For the other two types of reasons, however, there are only four; for in the case of a purely positive reason (*kevalānvayin*), because there is no dissimilar instance, there can be no exclusion from it.
Because there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*) for a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*), it is impossible for [the reason] to exist therein.
Among those reasons intended in their various forms, some are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) when they are associated with certain [defects] and devoid of others.

These are: the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), the unascertained (*anadhyavasita*), the mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), the counter-balanced (*satpratipakṣa*), and the neutralized by the context (*prakaraṇasama*).

In this context, *siddhi* (establishment) is the cognition of the property of being a subject-attribute (*pakṣadharmatva*) in that which is pervaded. Its absence is *asiddhi* (non-establishment). That which possesses it is *asiddha* (unestablished). It is of four kinds: unestablished due to lack of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*), unestablished due to the locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), unestablished due to the lack of the property of being a subject-attribute (*pakṣadharmatvāsiddha*), and unestablished due to the non-cognition of this [pervasion] (*etatpramityasiddha*). Among these, the unestablished due to lack of pervasion is...

It is of two kinds: that which lacks a connection with the probandum (*sādhyasambandharahita*), and that which possesses a connection based on a limiting condition (*sopādhikasambandha*). The first is, for example: "Everything is momentary because it exists. This is included within the category of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) due to the absence of a connection between both [the reason and the probandum].
The second is, for example: "Institutionalized violence (*vaidhī hiṃsā*) is a means to demerit (*adharma*), because it is violence, like the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahiṃsā*)."
This is because the condition (*upādhi*) of being prohibited exists in the relationship between the nature of violence and the means of demerit.

A condition is that which, while pervading the probandum (*sādhya*), also pervades the probans (*sādhana*). And "being prohibited" pervades the probandum, which is "being a means to demerit. Wherever there is being a means to demerit, [there is being prohibited].

This is because of the rule that "prohibitedness" [must be present]; however, it does not pervade the "nature of violence" (hiṃsātva) intended as the probans, since even though the nature of violence exists in the subject (pakṣa), prohibitedness is absent there. This, moreover, prior to the counter-argument, indicates a lack of pervasion regarding ritual violence (vaidhahiṃsā).
For "being prohibited," by ceasing because it does not pervade the probans (*sādhana*), and by causing [the opponent's reason] to cease because it pervades the probandum (*sādhya*),

brings about a connection between "being violence" (*hiṃsātva*) and the absence of the probandum. However, after the time of the counter-argument (*vipratipatti*), it becomes a raiser of a counter-position (*pratipakṣa*), since it ceases from the subject (*pakṣa*) while not pervading the probans.

The *upādhi* (limiting condition) excludes that [subject] because it pervades the *sādhya* (the probandum). Consequently, the absence of the *upādhi* becomes the reason (*hetu*) for proving the absence of the *sādhya*. For example: "Vedic ritual killing (*vaidhī hiṃsā*) is not a means for producing demerit (*adharma*), because it is not prohibited, like eating. And thus, when there is no pervasion due to the presence of an *upādhi*, the proposition (*pratijñā*) [is undermined].
And it is included within the category of "conflict between equally strong reasons" (*samabalavirodha*).

The unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*) is also of two kinds: that which has a non-existent locus and that which is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). An example of the first is: "A rabbit's horn is sharp, because it is a horn. This does not constitute a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) at all, because there is no example of it that is unmixed with contradictions such as those of valid cognition (*pramāṇavirodha*). An example of the second is, for one who denies the existence of God:

"The earth and so forth possess an agent because they are effects"—this [fallacy] is included within the category of *asaṅgata* (incoherence), because it proceeds toward establishing what is not required [by the context]. The *pakṣadharmatvāsiddha* (unestablished presence in the subject) is of many kinds; for example: "Sound is eternal because it is visible," and so forth.

In this regard, it has already been stated that the "unestablished due to a difference in locus" (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*) is not a fault. The "unestablished due to a useless qualifier" (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇāsiddha*) and the "unestablished due to a useless qualificand" (*vyarthaviśeṣyāsiddha*) are included within the category of "redundancy" (*adhikya*). As for the "unestablished due to an unestablished qualifier" (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇāsiddha*), it is not [listed as a separate fault] because there is no example of it that is unmixed with other faults, such as: "This earth is scratched by a rabbit's horn, because it is earth."

The fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*). The other [type], namely that which lacks the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), is included within the "unestablished" (*asiddha*). An example of this is the unestablished due to the non-apprehension of the cognition [of the reason]: "Because it possesses smoke," when there is no distinction between smoke and steam. This too is indeed unestablished. A reason that exists only in the subject and the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is the "contradictory" (*viruddha*). For example: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced. This too—

It is under-extended (*avyāpta*) because, while there is an absence of connection with the probandum (*sādhya*), it possesses a connection with its absence. That which occurs in the subject (*pakṣa*), the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For example: "Sound is eternal, because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*). This too is indeed under-extended, because it lacks connection with the probandum; for that which establishes the probandum must exist only in the subject.
The inconclusive reason (*anadhyavasita*) is of three kinds. Among these, that which lacks both similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is, for example:
"All things are impermanent, because they exist. That which possesses both is, for example: "The earth is eternal, because it possesses odor.
That which possesses similar instances but lacks dissimilar instances is, for example: "Sound is denotable, because it is sound. This...

Some maintain that because its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished, it is not a distinct fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Others, however, say: "The unestablished in pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*) is that which lacks both similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*); when a similar instance exists, it is that which occurs only in the subject (*pakṣa*). Both [types]—that which possesses a similar instance but lacks a dissimilar instance, and [the former]—are included within the 'inconclusive' (*anaikāntika*). For it is thus: the inconclusive is that which deviates (*savyabhicāra*).

Inconsistency (vyabhicāra) occurs both through positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka). In this context, the domain of positive concomitance consists of the subject (pakṣa) and the similar instances (sapakṣa). A reason that exists even outside of these—in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa)—is the common inconclusive (sādhāraṇānaikāntika). The domain of negative concomitance consists of the dissimilar instances;
it may also include a portion of the similar instances. In that regard, a reason that does not exist in any of the similar instances at all is the uncommon inconclusive (asādhāraṇānaikāntika).
In every respect, this falls within the category of "non-pervasion" (*avyāpti*), because of the absence of both types of relation.

Some maintain that this is not a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) because a negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is possible. Others, however, ask: even when a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) exists, does there exist any pervasion at all for that which does not occur therein? Or is it like a purely negative reason (*kevalavyatirekin*) where such pervasion exists?

They say that a reason is a fallacy (hetvābhāsa) because it invades doubt. A "neutralized" reason (prakaraṇasama) is one that possesses the three characteristics [of a valid reason] even though it establishes both the proponent's and the opponent's positions. For example: "The subject of dispute is false, because it is perceptible. This is because its truth could also be asserted; however, this [reason] is impossible [to establish definitively].

Some say: "That is incorrect; for [the fallacy] arises from mere conceit (abhimāna), like a true counter-thesis. This too is simply a contradiction of equal strength with the proposition (pratijñā). Since it is included within the fallacies of the thesis (pakṣābhāsa) or the fallacies of the reason (hetvābhāsa), it need not be mentioned separately. This is incorrect, because it manifests through the proposition alone.

Furthermore, in the case of a proof (*sādhana*), contradictions with one's own actions (*svakriyāvirodha*) and contradictions with one's own principles (*svanyāyavirodha*) are not included among the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

An example of contradiction with one's own action is: "I am mute. An example of contradiction with one's own principles is: "The object of cognition (*prameya*) is independent of the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
Thus, by subsuming even fallacious examples (*udāharaṇābhāsa*) within fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), they do not state that these must be mentioned separately.
For instance: fallacious examples are those lacking the defining characteristics of an example, yet appearing as if they were examples.
Among these, an example based on similarity (*sādharmya-udāharaṇa*) that is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*) is, for example: "The mind is impermanent because it is corporeal."

Whatever is corporeal is impermanent, such as an atom; this is an example [of a valid reason]. An example lacking the probans (*sādhanavikala*) is, for instance, "action" (*karman*). An example lacking both [the probandum and the probans] (*ubhayavikala*) is, for instance, "space" (*ākāśa*). An example lacking a locus (*āśrayahīna*) is, for instance, "the horn of a hare. An example of stating that which is non-pervasive (*avyāpti*) is, for instance, "like a jar."

An example of stating a reversed pervasion (*viparītavyāpti*) is: "Whatever is impermanent is corporeal, like a jar. An example where the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is not excluded in the instance of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyodāharaṇa*) is: "Whatever is not impermanent is not corporeal, like action (*karman*). An example where the probans (*sādhana*) is not excluded is: "like an atom (*paramāṇu*)."
An example of that which is not excluded from either [the subject or the predicate] is: "like a jar. An example of one lacking a locus is as previously described.
An example of stating an insufficient pervasion (*avyāpti*) is: "like space" (*ākāśa*). An example of stating a reversed pervasion (*viparītavyāpti*) is:
"whatever is not corporeal (*mūrta*) is not impermanent," as in "like space. In this case...

Since the citation of a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmyodāharaṇa*) is useless, the statement of its fallacious forms is likewise useless. Furthermore, the failure to state the pervasion (*avyāpti*) is neither a fault nor a deficiency; moreover, the statement of a reversed pervasion (*viparītavyāpti*) is also irrelevant. And the lack of a substratum (*āśrayahīnatva*) is not a defect, just like the unestablished nature of the substratum (*āśrayāsiddhi*); for the example is [already] defective by the deficiency of either one [of its required features].

Because it is defective, the deficiency of both [the probandum and the probans] is not to be counted separately. Therefore, there are only two types of defects in an example: the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) and the deficiency of the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*). Among these, when there is a deficiency of the probandum, the example becomes a counter-example (*vipakṣa*); in that case, the probans existing therein is either inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) or contradictory (*viruddha*).

[It] occurs. [Objection: "If there is a deficiency in the probans (*sādhana*), it is the 'unestablishedness of pervasion' (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*); thus, the fault of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*) is included within the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*). [Response: No, because it manifests immediately after the statement of the example.
This is because when a probans exists in another similar instance (*sapakṣa*) but does not exist in the similar instance that has been made the example, [the fault arises].

And because it is untenable for that [reason] to be a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). If it is argued that even there, because the pervasion has not been demonstrated, it is a case of "unestablished due to lack of pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*), we say no; for even so, there is no defect in the meaning (*artha*).
Thus ends [the work] composed by the venerable feet of Śrīmad Jayatīrtha.
The chapter on inference in the *Pramāṇapaddhati* is completed.
The section on scripture (*āgamapariccheda*):

the definition of scripture is that scripture is a faultless word. Its capacity to convey meaning consists in its being expressive, either through the absence of a denotable object or through the absence of a logical concomitance (*anvaya*).

Scripture (*āgama*) is speech free from defects such as: conveying a contrary understanding, making known what is already known, being purposeless, having an undesirable purpose, teaching a means that cannot be accomplished, or instructing in a cumbersome method when a simpler one exists; or, it is simply a sentence that is faultless.

A *pada* (word) consists of phonemes (*varṇa*) ending in a case-suffix. A *vākya* (sentence) is a collection of *padas* possessing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*). Expectancy is the desire to know; it is a property of conscious beings. Because they are the objects of that [desire], meanings are said to possess expectancy; and because they convey those meanings, words are also said to possess it. Proximity is the state of being uttered without delay.

The property of the word itself is [the absence of contradiction with valid cognition]. Compatibility (*yogyatā*)—the absence of contradiction with valid cognition for that which has a perceived syntactic connection—is a property of the word-meanings. Because they express those [meanings], words themselves are said to possess compatibility. In this regard, by means of being a word, there is the absence of a denotable object; by means of expectancy and proximity, there is the absence of syntactic connection; and by means of compatibility...
And once the possibility of conveying a contrary meaning has been refuted, the term "faultless" (*nirdoṣa*) is included for the purpose of excluding all defects.

The auditory organ, when in contact with the final phoneme, accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each preceding phoneme, and aided by the latent impressions of grasping the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*), generates a single cognition of a word (*padabuddhi*) even from among many phonemes. Similarly, the auditory organ, directed toward the final word and assisted by the latent impressions produced by the experience of each preceding word, [generates a single cognition] from among many words.

It generates the cognition of a sentence in accordance with expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and the other factors. By this means, the collection of phonemes (*varṇa*) and words (*pada*), even though they are perceived as not existing simultaneously, is rendered possible. Furthermore, traditional scripture (*āgama*)—which consists of the sacred word (*kūśruta*) and is supported by the recollection of convention (*samaya*)—is accompanied by an investigation into the logic of verbal expression.

Thus, it is the indicator of its own meaning, and not by its mere existence. The Bhāṭṭas hold that the genus (*jāti*) alone is the denotable object of words, while individuals (*vyakti*) are indicated (*lakṣya*). The Vaiśeṣikas hold that individuals qualified by the genus are the denotable objects.
The Grammarians (*Vaiyākaraṇas*) hold that in some cases it is the genus and in others it is the individual. [In other cases] it is the genus, and in others it is the individual.

In some cases, the Naiyāyikas maintain that it is the generic form (*ākṛti*); the Buddhists hold that it is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*); and the Teachers (*ācāryas*) maintain that the individuals themselves are what are denoted, while similarity serves as a basis for the cognition of the convention. This is an investigation regarding the object that conveys the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Objection: Is it not the case that what is called "convention" (*samaya*) is the relationship of signifier and signified between words and their meanings? And since that relationship cannot be known as long as the related entities are unknown, the knowledge of word-meanings is already established even prior to [the study of] scripture; therefore, what is the purpose of scripture? It is replied: Just as even when two things are already known...

The relation between the property and the locus is understood through inference; likewise, scripture is the means of understanding the specific relations among objects already known. If it is argued that since words have only individual word-meanings as their object, there is nothing that can convey the understanding of their mutual relation (*anvaya*), [the response follows here].

The Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas) maintain that the word known as *sphoṭa*—indivisible and manifested by means of phonemes (*varṇa*) and words—is what conveys the understanding of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*). Others say it is a mere series of phonemes. Still others claim it is the final phoneme of the sentence.

Some hold that it is the proximity (*sānnidhya*) of the words. And yet others assert that it is the word-meanings themselves, as denoted by the words, when they possess expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and the other necessary conditions.

Thus say the Bhāṭṭas. Since all these positions lack scriptural authority and contradict valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the discerning hold that words themselves denote their own meanings as already related (*anvita*). Among them, the Prābhākaras maintain that each word individually is capable of denoting its specific relation; that is, each [word] denotes [the meaning] in a general sense.

The Teachers maintain that words, which possess the power to denote their own meanings as connected with what is either compatible or incompatible, acquire further powers through the proximity of other words and thus denote their own meanings specifically as already connected, because such is our experience;
this constitutes the twofold nature of verbal testimony (*āgama*).

Scripture (*āgama*) is of two kinds: non-human (*apauruṣeya*) and human (*pauruṣeya*). Among these, the Veda is non-human, while the other is human. Phonemes (*varṇa*) are everywhere immutable and eternal, and they are all-pervading (*sarvagata*). Words (*pada*) as well are strictly fixed; their relation to word-meanings (*padārtha*) is likewise inherent (*svābhāvika*). Nevertheless, in a sentence (*vākya*)—
This distinction arises from the presence or absence of the quality of being preceded by an independent person (*svatantra-puruṣa*) in the specific sequence of words.

Regarding the proof that scripture (*āgama*) is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that scripture is merely included within inference (*anumāna*). That is incorrect.

The Prābhākaras maintain that because the cognition of the meaning of a sentence is experienced even without the consideration of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, the non-human (Vedic) word is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas the human (secular) word is inference. This too is incorrect, because there is no reason to postulate a distinction between the two when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is identical in both cases. Thus, these [means of valid cognition] are only three.

Presumption (arthāpatti) is included within inference; indeed, presumption and the others are included among these [means of knowledge]. For instance, presumption is the cognition of that which makes an observed fact possible, arising from the observation of a fact that would otherwise be inexplicable. For example, when there is the knowledge that "Caitra, being alive, is not at home," [the presumption arises that he is outside].

Knowledge of external existence. Although here it is not possible for each [reason] individually to serve as a mark for external existence due to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), nevertheless: Caitra exists outside, because while being alive, he is not in the house.
Whoever is alive and is not in a certain place exists elsewhere than that; just as, for example, I do.
The status of being a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the two—existence and the absence of a house—is indeed established when they are conjoined.
If it is argued that there is an impossibility of a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) between two contradictory things, we say no;
for non-contradiction between the general and the particular is observed even within the same entity. This is because absolute contradiction [does not apply here].
Nor does presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) apply here; rather, through contradiction, there is only doubt.

Comparison (*upamāna*) is the means for the cognition of similarity. In that regard, a cognition such as "this is similar to that" or "these two are similar" is born of perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, a cognition such as "the cow and the gavaya are similar," which arises from a statement, is simply scripture (*āgama*).

When one perceives the similarity residing in the remembered object while perceiving the perceived object, and thereby cognizes the similarity residing in the perceived object within that which is being remembered, this is indeed inference (*anumāna*). If it is objected: "The similarity, as it is apprehended as residing in the perceived object, is the instrument (*karaṇa*); whereas that which resides in the remembered object is the object of cognition (*prameya*). Therefore, how can there be the relationship of mark and what-is-marked (*liṅga-liṅgibhāva*) between these two, which reside in different loci?"—we reply: No, for [the inference is formulated as]: "That cow is similar to this gavaya; because of this gavaya... [and so forth].

Because it resembles that [cow]. Whatever resembles something else resembles that very thing; for example, as Yama [resembles] another Yama. Since this universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) is possible, there is no fault in the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

Alternatively, the state of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) of a resemblance not residing in the subject itself serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*), and thus there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

The means of valid cognition for non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*) is that which causes the knowledge of non-existence. In this regard, the current non-existence of the Kauravas and others is understood from the traditional scripture (*āgama*) such as the *Mahābhārata*. The absence of Devadatta’s eyes and other sense organs is to be inferred from the mark (*liṅga*) of not perceiving visible forms and so forth.

The cognition of the absence of pleasure and so forth occurs through the direct perception of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*) alone. However, the cognition of the absence of a jar or similar object situated in front of one, which arises instantaneously, is indeed the result of direct perception itself; it is not produced by mere non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), because it is a form of immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*). Non-apprehension, in this context, is merely the unavoidable presence [of conditions for perception]. This is the case where, in the dark...

Through the act of searching, such as stretching out one's hand, one cognizes the absence of a jar; at that time, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is not the instrument (*karaṇa*). Rather, in this case, the jar is known to be absent precisely by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*), because it is not apprehended despite being capable of being perceived. In the same way, the cognition of the absence of an elephant and so forth in the morning is produced by the logical mark of non-apprehension.

If it is argued that there is no possibility of sensory contact with a non-entity (*abhāva*), we say no; for there is no subverting factor against the sensory contact of a non-entity just as there is for an entity (*bhāva*). Limited knowledge is possible within extensive knowledge; for example, when one knows "there are one hundred," the abandonment of [the notion of] "fifty" occurs. That too is indeed inference: Devadatta possesses fifty, because he possesses one hundred.

This is because the application [of the term] "I" is possible. *Pariśeṣa* (presumption by elimination) is the cognition that arises when, after negating what is applicable, something remains. For example, when there is the knowledge that "these two are Devadatta and Yajñadatta," upon the negation "this one is not Yajñadatta," the cognition of Devadatta arises. This is produced by inference: "This is Devadatta..."

Because, while being one of the two—Devadatta or Yajñadatta—he is not Yajñadatta; for the application [of this reasoning] is valid through the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*), as in the case of Yajñadatta. The *upakrama* and other such [criteria] are also merely forms of inference.
Tradition (*aitihya*) is a succession of reports whose original speaker is unspecified, such as: "In this banyan tree..."

The statement "Vaiśravaṇa exists" is itself an authoritative source (āgama). In this way, other means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) as well should be subsumed within those already mentioned. This concludes the determination of the validity of the means of valid cognition.

If it is asked, "By what is the validity of these means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) produced, and by what is their invalidity known?"—it is replied: regarding this, the Sāṅkhyas maintain that both [validity and invalidity] of cognitions arise from themselves alone (*svataḥ*). In this context, "arising from itself" (*svatastva*) with respect to production means not depending on any cause other than that which produces the cognition itself.

Self-validity (*svatastva*) regarding cognition consists in its independence from any cognizer other than the cognition itself and its means of cognition. The Naiyāyikas and others maintain that both [production and apprehension] are extrinsic (*parataḥ*). Extrinsicness regarding production (*utpatti*) consists in being produced by causes other than those that produce the cognition.
Extrinsicness regarding apprehension (*jñapti*) consists in dependence upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) other than the cognition itself and its cognizer. In this regard:

Knowledge is produced by the sense organs and so forth; validity, moreover, is produced by the excellence (*guṇa*) of the sense organs and so forth; likewise, invalidity is produced by their defects (*doṣa*). Thus, knowledge is cognizable through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*); therein, validity and invalidity are to be inferred from the signs of correspondence (*saṃvāda*) and non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*). The Buddhists maintain that validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*) and invalidity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*).

Even the Bhāṭṭas, who accept the position that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) and invalidity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*), maintain that in the case of cognition, validity as a qualifier is inferred through the specific quality of "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*); thus, they consider validity to be intrinsic in its apprehension (*jñapti*).
However, they hold that invalidity is extrinsic, as it is known through other means of inference such as non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*).

The Prābhākaras maintain that the cognition qualified by validity is established by self-luminous knowledge (*svaprakāśajñāna*) alone; indeed, invalidity does not exist at all. Rather, a cognition qualified by validity arises from the sense organs and other factors alone; qualities (*guṇa*), however, are of no consequence. Invalidity, on the other hand, arises from the sense organs and other factors when they are assisted by defects (*doṣa*).

Likewise, both that cognition and its validity are known by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) alone. The masters maintain that while the mere nature of an invalid cognition is cognizable by the witness, its invalidity is to be inferred. However, the very capacity of the instruments [of knowledge] to produce cognition—which is acquired from their own causes—is itself the capacity to produce validity.

However, another power, arising through the influence of defects (*doṣa*), manifests for the production of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). But the cognition [of validity] arises from something else (*parataḥ*) alone;

for the essential nature of the sense organs and so forth is known by their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and their status as the instruments for producing knowledge of reality is known through inference. Such being the case, by means of these pramāṇas...
Having ascertained the eternality, non-eternality, and so forth of categories of existence, one who has become dispassionate toward sense-objects,

who possesses the perfection of tranquility, self-restraint, and the like, who has taken refuge solely in Vāsudeva, and who has practiced for a long time with devotion and continuity the hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption directed toward Him—

When there is direct realization of the Blessed One, through an intensely elevated devotion, liberation occurs by the grace of the Blessed One, characterized by the manifestation of one's own nature as bliss and so forth, distinguished by the cessation of all that is undesirable. May this *Pramāṇapaddhati*, composed by the lord of sages Jayatīrtha for the instruction of the simple-minded, bring delight to Mādhava and Madhva.
Thus ends the section on Scripture (*āgama*) in the *Pramāṇapaddhati* composed by the venerable Śrī Jayatīrtha.
This work is also complete.
